As envisaged in Plato, the cities of the Republic are characterized by a unique property regime and a community of wives of guardians, as well as by the absence of statutory law. This social structure includes a common diet and gymnasium, which, while beneficial in many ways, can become dangerous in the event of civil strife, as evidenced by the youth cases of Miletus, Boeotia and Thurii. Moreover, Plato believes that a long-term system may corrupt the natural pleasure of love, which is shared not only by humans but also by animals. He considered that the cantons, particularly those that encouraged the use of gymnasiums, were primarily responsible for such corruption. Plato also noted that, while the pleasures experienced during childbirth were considered natural, the pleasures generated by same-sex relationships were seen as contrary to nature. He accused the Creetans of fabricating the story of Ganymede to justify their “unnatural happiness.” The Republic is a dialogue between Socrates and several young people to explore all aspects of the ideal society. Instead, the Law is a discussion among three older men who designed a reproductive law strategy to hide their rhetorical tactics of piety, ritualism and virtue from the younger generation. Plato recognizes the existence of a device in the law, as he said, “I know a device in the law.” In short, as Plato describes, the Republic city is a complex society with unique institutions and values. While its aim is to build an ideal State, it also faces potential challenges and criticism, particularly with regard to the approach to love and relationships.

The term “opposition office” is often associated with prestige and authority in a professional environment. It typically refers to the office space located at the corner of a building, which is usually reserved for high-ranking executives or senior managers. The phrase has been used in various contexts, reflecting its significance in the corporate world. The “Market Square” radio programme in the United States public media included a section called “Convection of Corner Offices”, where chief executive officers from different industries shared their insights and experiences. This recurring segment highlights the importance of leadership and decision-making in various sectors. Richard Conniff, in his book, the Office of the Apes of the Corner, explored the application of evolutionary biology and sociobiology theory in the concept of workplace management. The book delves into the behavioral patterns and dynamics that can be observed in office environments, drawing parallels with the natural world. In the entertainment industry, the term "corner office" has also made its way into popular culture. For instance, the law-drama series "Suits" frequently references the corner office, emphasizing the status and influence that come with occupying such a space. The series showcases the competitive nature of the legal profession and the desire to reach the top. Additionally, "Corner Office" is a 2022 black comedy film directed by Joachim Back and starring Jon Hamm. The film's narrative revolves around the concept of the corner office, further emphasizing its symbolic value in the corporate world. The phrase "corner office" has also been used in music, with "Corner Office Bedroom" being a song by the band PlayRadioPlay!. This demonstrates the widespread recognition and cultural impact of the term. In literature, the concept of the corner office has been explored in various books. Dr. Lois P. Frankel's "Nice Girls Don't Get the Corner Office: 101 Unconscious Mistakes Women Make That Sabotage Their Careers" discusses the challenges faced by women in the corporate world and the unconscious biases that can hinder their progress. The book provides valuable advice to women seeking to advance their careers and break the glass ceiling. Furthermore, David Leonhardt's article "Who's in the Corner Office?" published in The New York Times, delves into the characteristics and qualities of individuals who occupy these prestigious positions. The article examines the factors that contribute to their success and the responsibilities they hold. Valerie Young's "The Secret Thoughts of Successful Women" also touches upon the topic, discussing the mindset and strategies that have helped women achieve success in their careers. The book provides an in-depth look at the thought processes and behaviors that contribute to professional growth. In summary, the "corner office" is a term that has permeated various aspects of society, from business and management to entertainment and literature. It symbolizes the highest marks of professional achievement and the desire to reach the top of the corporate ladder.

The Association for Law, Property, and Society is a scholarly organization in the United States dedicated to the study of property law and its social implications. Established to foster research and dialogue in this field, the association brings together academics, professionals, and students. One of the primary activities of the association is organizing an annual conference. The inaugural edition of this conference was held at Georgetown Law in 2010, marking the beginning of a tradition that continues to provide a platform for the exchange of ideas and scholarly debate. In addition to the conference, the Association for Law, Property, and Society is also the publisher of the academic journal "Law, Property and Society." This journal serves as a forum for the dissemination of research findings and scholarly articles that contribute to the understanding of property law and its intersection with societal issues. As of the latest update, the leadership of the association is held by Tim Mulvaney, who is a faculty member at Texas A&M University. His role as Chairman involved monitoring the activities of the organization and ensuring its continued relevance and contributing to the field of property law and social research. The Association for Law, Property, and Society plays a vital role in advancing the understanding of property law and its impact on society, providing a valuable resource for those interested in this area of legal scholarship.

This paper introduces the concept of the implied Sharpe ratio, a novel measure of a European option's attractiveness to an investor. The Sharp Ratio, which is usually used to evaluate the performance of the Common Fund, is adjusted here to assess the value of the various options in the portfolio. The paper builds upon seminal works by Sharpe, Jensen, Merton, and others, who have explored the performance of investment portfolios and the impact of risk on asset returns. The implied Sharpe ratio is defined in relation to the Merton value function, which represents the maximum expected utility of an investor's wealth under the assumption of a geometric Brownian motion for the risky asset. The implied Sharpe ratio is the unique positive solution that equates the investor's value function in a general market setting with the Merton value function. This innovative concept allows investors to evaluate European options based on their potential to enhance expected terminal utility, rather than relying solely on implied volatility, which does not capture an option's worth relative to an investor's utility. This paper provides an overall framework for the calculation of the implicit Sharp ratios applicable in any market environment, and provides an equation for the ratios based on model parameters and investor risk avoidance parameters. Using a Taylor series expansion technique, the authors develop semi-explicit approximations of the implied Sharpe ratio, facilitating its calculation under various local stochastic volatility models. The author has demonstrated the practical application of the implicit Sharp Ratio by demonstrating its usefulness in identifying the most appropriate European investment options among the available options. The paper's contribution lies in providing investors with a new tool for assessing the value of European options in the context of their overall investment strategy, taking into account the investor's risk preferences and the specific characteristics of the options under consideration.

In December 1980, the concept of special aid resource teachers was introduced, with the aim of identifying and addressing the literacy and numeracy deficiencies of individual children. This approach was supported by various major committees of inquiry and their respective reports. Key reports that influenced this educational philosophy include: 1. The Bullock Report (1975) - A UK Committee of Inquiry appointed by the Secretary of State for Education and Science. 2. The Cadman Report (1976) - A report by the Australian Parliament's House of Representatives Select Committee on Specific Learning Difficulties. 3. The 1977 Report of the Working Party on Provisions for Children with Special Needs in the Australian Capital Territory (ACT). 4. The Warnock Report (1978) - A UK Committee of Inquiry into the Education of Handicapped Children and Young People. 5. Report of Task Force 8 (1979) - presented to Victorian Special Education Commission. 6. The Victorian Ministerial Committee on Special Assistance Programs' Report (1980). The educational philosophy that underpinned the Special Assistance Program was deeply rooted in these reports. It emphasized the significant impact of a child's learning environment on their behavior and learning. Furthermore, it recognized the importance of meeting children's learning needs within a shared structural and social framework. This perspective led to the development of programs that provided resources and assistance to classroom teachers, enabling them to better support students with specific learning challenges.

Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) is a mandatory health insurance scheme for international students studying in Australia, as stipulated by the Australian Government. This insurance provides coverage similar to that provided by the Australian health care system, ensuring that students have access to the necessary health services while in the country. International students may choose to arrange their occupational safety and health allowances through their own educational institutions. However, they are not limited to providers recommended by the institution. Students can independently choose the OSHC provider of their choice, even if the institution has a preferred provider arrangement with a particular insurer. Only Australian private health insurers who have entered into a Deed with the Australian government are authorized to offer OSHC. This Deed outlines the essential conditions that registered insurers must meet to provide the OSHC product. As a legal agreement between the Commonwealth of Australia and the respective insurer, the Deed specifies the minimum benefits that must be covered by the insurer. It also delineates the circumstances under which the insurer is exempt from providing benefits. Furthermore, clause 6.8 of the Deed outlines the conditions under which insurers can terminate policies and issue refunds. These conditions include: 1. If a student decides not to come to Australia. 2. If the student ceases to study and leaves Australia before the expiry of the visa. 3. If a student's application for an extended stay is denied by the Department of Home Affairs. OSHC aims to ensure that international students have access to health services during their stay in Australia, providing mental calm and financial protection during their studies.

School uniforms are standardized clothing for students, mainly in educational institutions such as schools. These uniforms are prevalent in primary and secondary schools across various countries. Typical school uniforms may include shirts, pants for boys, clothes, skirts for girls and coats for men and women. Alternatively, uniforms can be simple enough to require the wearing of shirts, limit the colour selection or limit the type of clothing that students can wear. It is important to note the distinction between dress codes and school uniforms. According to scholars such as Nathan Joseph, clothing can be considered a uniform only if: (a) it is used as a group emblem, (b) the legitimacy of an institution is demonstrated by disclosure of the relative status of the individual, and (c) the personality is suppressed. On the contrary, as Marian Wilde has pointed out, dress codes are less restrictive and focus on promoting modesty and discouraging anti-social fashion speech. The clothing code may include rules such as the prohibition on tearing clothes, the prohibition on marking or limiting the amount of skin exposure. School uniforms are unique to each level of education, and each institution often has its own unique design. The history of school uniforms is not easy to trace, as there is no comprehensive written statement. However, it is believed that the practice of wearing uniforms in schools has a long-standing tradition with various known influences.

Our research explored the fractal nature of profit landscapes in financial markets, comparing actual market data with various human time series models. We scrutinized the scaling behaviour of the highest local standard ($M) relative to the resolution parameter ($N) and found that it followed the scaling behaviour of the power-law relationship ($M\sim Na). Interestingly, actual market data show a proportionally scaled index of about $1.6 million, but this index is not replicated by models with short-term return distribution, such as geo-brown and brown fraction movements. However, the models containing the pattern of back-to-back returns, in particular log-fixed power methods and polyfractal stacking models, successfully replicated the observed scaling index. Notably, our analysis of the LP model reveals that the heavy-tail of the return distribution is the primary driver of the fractality observed in the profit landscape. Our research also explores the maximum attainable value of the scaling exponent $a$ within the MSM, suggesting a potential upper limit of $a \approx 1.6$. This interesting observation opens the way for future research to understand the root causes of such behaviour. Additionally, we demonstrate that the fractal nature of the profit landscape is largely independent of long-term memory effects in the time series, as evidenced by the preservation of the scaling exponent even after shuffling the time series to eliminate long-term correlations. The innovative aspect of our study, which is that determining the end of the distribution of proceeds is a key factor in the fragmentation of profit patterns, has a significant impact on the validation of the time-series model of stock prices. By adjusting model parameters, such as LP$\alpha$ and MSM$_$0, researchers can align the scores of the manual time series with those observed in the actual market, thereby enhancing the realistic and predictive capabilities of the models. In conclusion, our work highlights the importance of heavy-tailed return distributions in financial markets and their role in shaping the fractal characteristics of profit landscapes. This insight can guide the development of more accurate and reliable financial time series analysis models. We thank the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) for its support in facilitating this study.

The importance of understanding human rights and the programmes implemented to protect them cannot be overemphasized. In this regard, education plays a key role, as it aims to inform beneficiaries about their human rights and the efforts of non-governmental organizations and other entities to strengthen these rights. In addition, education helps Governments, international organizations and donor agencies to understand their roles and responsibilities in upholding human rights. The right to participation is one of the key principles in this area. This principle emphasizes the importance of including beneficiaries in the planning and implementation of programs designed to benefit them. By involving beneficiaries, organizations can empower them and ensure that their needs and perspectives are taken into account. Another key principle is accountability. This principle establishes standards for human rights and development, holding NGOs, international organizations, donor agencies, and governments to higher standards of responsibility. Accountability ensures that these entities are transparent, efficient, and effective in their efforts to promote and protect human rights. Several NGOs have been traditionally involved in advocating for human rights. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch are two such organizations that have expanded their focus from political rights to include economic and social rights as well. This expansion reflects the growing recognition of the interconnectedness of various types of rights and the need for a comprehensive approach to human rights advocacy. Oxfam is another non-governmental organization that adopts a rights-based approach to development. This organization has committed to not only providing relief to those in need but also addressing the structural causes of poverty and injustice. Oxfam does so to address the root causes of these problems and to create lasting and sustainable change. This approach integrates poverty, human rights, development and trade within the same framework and reflects a comprehensive and holistic understanding of the challenges faced by marginalized communities. In conclusion, the promotion and protection of human rights require a multifaceted approach that includes education, participation, and accountability. NGOs play a vital role in this process, advocating for the rights of individuals and communities and working towards a more just and equitable world. By adopting rights-based approaches, these organizations can effectively address the complex issues surrounding human rights and development.

The Wallace Clark Award, also known as the Wallace Clark Medal, was a prestigious honor bestowed upon individuals for their Distinguished Contribution to Scientific Management. This honour was won by Henry Wallace Clark (1880-1948), a prominent figure in the field of scientific management. Established in 1949, the award is supported by several well-known organizations, including the American Management Association, the American Society of Mechanical Engineers, the Association of Consulting Management Engineers and the Society for the Advancement of Management. These organizations recognized the importance of scientific management and its impact on various industries. The first recipient of the Wallace Clark Medal was Swiss Hugo de Haan in 1948. At the time, de Haan held the position of executive secretary for the Comite International de l'Organisation Scientifique (CIOS). CIOS is an organization dedicated to promoting global scientific management. It was founded during the first International Management Congress in Prague in 1924, which aimed to foster the advancement of management practices worldwide. The Wallace Clark Award celebrates the achievements of individuals who have made significant contributions to the field of scientific management, highlighting their impact on improving efficiency and effectiveness across sectors. The award is testimony to the current commitment to excellence in management practices and to the continued pursuit of innovation in this area.

Strategic planning is a critical process for organizations, focusing on the development and implementation of long-term goals and objectives. It involves a comprehensive analysis of the current business environment, the identification of potential opportunities and threats, and the formulation of strategies to achieve desired outcomes. One key aspect of strategic planning is the concept of "strategic windows," which emphasizes the importance of timing in the execution of strategies. The entry and exit points of the strategy must be carefully considered in order to maximize its effectiveness. This concept has led some strategic planners to incorporate planned obsolescence into their strategies, allowing for the natural evolution and replacement of strategies over time. In 1983, Noel Tichy highlighted the challenges of habitual thinking in strategic planning. He argued that our natural tendency to repeat familiar patterns can limit creativity, hinder the exploration of new ideas, and impede our ability to address complex issues. To overcome these challenges, Tic proposed a systematic approach to reform, which includes a review of new issues in terms of technology and production, political and resource allocation, and corporate culture. Charles Handy, in 1989, identified two types of change in organizations: "strategic drift" and "transformational change." Strategic drift refers to a gradual change that occurs so subtly that it often goes unnoticed until it is too late. On the other hand, transformational change is sudden and radical, often triggered by major disruptions in the business environment or external shocks. Andy Grove, in the same year, introduced the term "strategic inflection point" to describe the moment when a new trend or direction is initiated. These inflection points can be either subtle or radical, depending on the nature of the change. Richard Pascale, in 1990, emphasized the need for continuous reinvention in the face of relentless change. He noted that “success and failure” implied that if organizations relied too much on success, past success could be a source of future weaknesses. This highlights the importance of constantly adapting and evolving strategies to stay ahead in a dynamic business landscape. In summary, strategic planning is a complex and ongoing process that requires organizations to be agile, innovative, and adaptable. By understanding the concepts of strategic windows, planned obsolescence, and the different types of change, organizations can better navigate the challenges of a rapidly changing business environment and ensure their long-term success.

The articles discussed the integration of information technology into higher education, highlighting various initiatives and their impact on learning experiences. The OECD Electronics Report Series provides a comprehensive review of video and remote text experiences in the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, questioning the view that United States agencies did not explore the potential of online education systems before the advent of the network. At Stanford University, the Faculty Authoring Development Program and Courseware Authoring Tools Project (1984–1990s) led to the creation of numerous teaching applications. These applications include a wide range of subjects, including economics coaching, theatre simulation, courses in thermals, history and anthropological role-playing. This initiative demonstrates the potential of technology to enhance educational experience. Reference was also made to a project at Carnegie-Mellon University, where IBM and the University had established a networked personal computer that benefited students and teachers. Similarly, at the University of Waterloo, IBM personal computers have established networks to facilitate work and application development, one of which is a web-based document server. These examples illustrate the growing adoption of technology in academic settings. OECD organized a conference in Paris, France, entitled “Education and new information technologies”, which further emphasized the importance of integrating technology into education. In addition, the Antic magazine reviewed the cartridges of Atari home computers so that users could access the CDC PLATO software through modems. This development demonstrates the growing reach of educational technologies beyond traditional academic institutions. Computer Teaching Corporation (CTC) played a significant role in the field by launching TenCORE, a leading authoring language in the late 1980s. TenCORE was MS-DOS based and enabled the creation of network-based applications, further demonstrating the growing sophistication of educational technology during this period. In short, the article highlights the progressive integration of information technology into higher education, with initiatives and projects demonstrating the potential of technology to transform learning experiences. The efforts of organizations such as OECD, universities and the CTC have contributed to the development and adoption of innovative educational tools and platforms.

The World Life Church (ULC) is a religious organization that provides online authorization to individuals wishing to become ministers. The ministers were then able to hold various religious ceremonies, including marriage ceremonies. The ULC's ministers are recognized in several states across the United States, and the laws regarding their authority to solemnize marriages vary from state to state. In Alaska, marriages can be solemnized by a minister, priest, or rabbi of any church or congregation within the state, or by the principal officer or elder of recognized churches or congregations that traditionally do not have regular ministers, priests, or rabbis. In addition, marriage may take place before or during any religious organization or assembly in accordance with the established ritual or form normally used in the organization or assembly. As of 2011, no court or administrative decision in Alaska excluded the person appointed as Minister of the Union of Legal Advisers. In Arizona, the person authorized to marry includes a duly authorized or appointed priest. As of 2011, no court or administrative ruling in Arizona had excluded those ordained as ministers of the ULC. Arkansas law allows for the solemnization of marriage by any regularly ordained minister or priest of any religious sect or denomination. As of 2011, there were no courts or administrative decisions in Arkansas that excluded the person appointed as Minister of the Uganda Joint Legal Centre. In California, a marriage may be solemnized by a priest, minister, rabbi, or authorized person. The specific requirements for authorization may vary, but the ULC's ministers are recognized in the state. It is important to note that the recognition of ULC Minister and his authority to perform marriage may change over time, in consultation with local authorities or legal experts, to ensure compliance with existing laws and regulations is always desirable.

Sporadic learning has a rich history, dating back to the end of the nineteenth century, when formal correspondence education, also known as distance learning, was used to first integrate physically remote learners into educational opportunities using the postal system. This marked the beginning of a new era in education, allowing students to learn independently and at their own pace. The 1920s and 1930s brought about significant advancements in the field, with the introduction of recorded audio. This development has led to a loss of synchronization of broadcasting and has significantly increased the scale of information dissemination. It allowed educational content to reach a wider audience, breaking the barriers of time and location. A major milestone in the distribution of standardized educational content occurred during World War II. The US military branches produced hundreds of training films, which were screened millions of times, ensuring that soldiers received consistent and standardized education regardless of their location. The advent of non-synchronous online learning dates back to the early 1980s, when schools and universities began investing heavily in computer technology. Pioneering applications such as Seymour Papert's Logo programming language enabled students to learn at their own pace, without being confined to the synchronous constraints of a traditional classroom lecture. As computers became more accessible and schools started connecting to the emerging Internet, asynchronous learning networks began to take shape. These networks supplemented existing classroom learning and gave rise to a new correspondence model for solitary learners. Students could now access online resources and communicate asynchronously through email and discussion boards. In the 1990s, the first tele-motion took place, with universities offering courses and the entire degree programme through a combination of simultaneous and non-synchronous online teaching. This marks a significant change in the way education is conducted, making it more flexible and more accessible to a wider range of learners. Today, non-synchronous learning is further developed with the integration of advanced multimedia technologies. These innovations have enhanced the learning experience, providing students with a wealth of resources and tools to facilitate independent learning and collaboration, regardless of their geographical location or time constraints.

Business schools often have different criteria for admission to their MBA programs, and entrance exam scores are not always required. Instead, the aim of these institutions is to create diversified classes by taking into account, among other things, the target gender ratio and the balance between local and international students. In some rare cases, an undergraduate degree is not mandatory for MBA admission, and significant management experience can be accepted as an alternative. For instance, in the UK, a Higher National Diploma (HND) or a Higher National Certificate (HNC) is considered acceptable by some programs. Work experience is a key component of the admission process for many MBA programmes. The type and duration of work experience can significantly influence an applicant's chances of admission. Top-tier programs typically require applicants to have at least five or more years of work experience. Future methyl bromide management applicants, particularly in the United States, are increasingly using methyl bromide management advisory services. In 2016, it was reported that up to one quarter of applicants were using these services, and that other countries, including India and Canada, were becoming increasingly popular. These consultants provide a range of services, such as assistance in the selection of options, mock interviews and essay proofreading. Some provide even more comprehensive services, such as writing from scratch. However, many of the enrolment committees in business schools often find the use of counselling services to be unfavourable. Applications may be negatively impacted if they appear to have been written with the help of a consultant. This can happen if the writing quality is significantly higher than the candidate's spoken language or if the application lacks uniqueness. It is essential for applicants to present their genuine skills and experiences in their applications to increase their chances of admission to MBA programs.

Higher Education Act 2004 (c) 8) is a piece of legislation passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom, which significantly reformed the higher education system in the UK, particularly in England and Wales. The Act's most notable and contentious provisions pertain to changes in university funding and the implementation of tuition fees. It is important to note that university funding falls within the jurisdiction of Northern Ireland and Scotland and is therefore not affected by the Act. The Act was the culmination of extensive and often heated debates. The Commission received Royal Assent on 1 July 2004. Until 1998, higher education in the United Kingdom, including university courses, was free of charge. However, the Labour Party, under the leadership of Prime Minister Tony Blair, abolished the student maintenance grant system and introduced an upfront fee of over £1,000 per year for all university students. While a portion of this fee was waived for the most financially disadvantaged students, critics argued that this move would burden students with unnecessary debt and detract from the principle of free public education. The Government maintains that the collection of fees is essential for the University to be adequately funded. At the same time, they set a target of increasing the proportion of students in higher education to 50 per cent by 2010. Over time, it is clear that the initial charge of approximately Pound1,000 per year is not sufficient to meet the funding needs of the University, leading to further reform proposals.

Productive resources are essential components in an economy, contributing to its overall output and growth. In some economic situations, when the Government increases its spending, it can use resources that would otherwise have been allocated to the private sector. This may lead to what is termed “crowding out”, and increased government spending will not lead to an increase in total economic output. Economists differ in their views on the importance of exclusion, with some considering it to be a long-term concern, while others view it as a minor problem, especially during periods of economic depression. Critics of fiscal policy often refer to the concept of Costa Rica as equivalent, assuming that the increase in government debt will ultimately require higher future taxes to service the debt. This expectation of future tax increases may lead individuals to reduce their current consumption, increase savings and prepare for higher tax rates. Thus, in Costa Rica, on an equal footing, any tax-deduction demand stimulus can be offset by increased savings to compensate for future tax liabilities. Economic inequality includes a range of disparities, including income inequality (measured by individual income distribution) and wealth inequality (assessed by wealth ownership distribution). Inequality can manifest itself in various forms, such as differences in consumption, land ownership and human capital, and can be observed at different levels, including between countries, groups and individuals. Several methods of quantifying inequality exist, among which the Gini coefficient is a recognized measure of individual income differentials. Another example is the Inequality Adjustment Human Development Index, a composite index that incorporates the inequality factor in order to provide a more comprehensive assessment of a country ' s development. Key concepts related to equality include equity, which emphasizes equity and justice in the allocation of resources and opportunities. Understanding and addressing economic inequalities is critical to promoting social cohesion and ensuring sustainable development.

The history of women in academia has many milestones and achievements. One notable pioneer was the first recorded woman to earn a doctorate in science. She worked at the University of Bologna and became the first salaried female university teacher, at one point being the highest paid employee there. In 1732, she made history again by becoming the first woman member of a scientific establishment, when she was elected to the Academy of Sciences of the Institute of Bologna. In 1764, Catherine II of Russia founded the Smorney High School for Women, which was recognized as the first State-funded higher education institution for women in Europe. The Commission of National Education in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, founded in 1777, is considered the first Ministry of Education in history. It is a central self-governing body responsible for national, secular and co-educational training. At the end of the nineteenth century, the University of Feiley appeared in the Russian province of Poland. This underground institution was created because women lacked access to higher education. Polish scholars and academics covertly taught women at this institution. Among its most famous students was Maria Skłodowska-Curie, better known as Marie Curie, who would later win two Nobel Prizes. Women ' s education is often provided through religious institutions. However, not all of these institutions focus solely on preparing women for marriage and childbirth. For example, the Quakers, from their foundation in the mid-17th century, held more egalitarian views on women, allowing for greater equality in education and other aspects of life. Outside of religious contexts, the Newington Academy for Girls was established in 1824 by abolitionists William Allen and his wife Grizell Hoare. It represents a further step forward in providing educational opportunities to women, further challenging social norms and expectations.

Dear Reader, We kindly request that you promptly complete and return the enclosed forms. The first is the recognition of any outstanding obligations and the name of the books of accounts to which the statements are presented, which should be filled in on the attached blanks (blank blues). The second form is used to update our records (yellow blanks). Lastly, please send us a postal money order for the amount of money you can spare at this time. We urge you to fill in and deliver the forms as soon as possible. On May 15, 1906, we received timely returns of money and acknowledgments, which were both encouraging and prompt. Surprisingly, some of those initially considered suspicious were the first to acknowledge their debts. Eventually, they were able to reproduce their books, and the acknowledged balances almost matched their estimated total of good accounts. Remittances continued until over $170,000 was paid. Approximately $25,000 of this amount covered accounts that were not included in their estimate of collectible indebtedness. This increased their estimated total to $200,000, confirming that more than eighty-five percent of all owed debts were acknowledged promptly under this call on honor. Four years later, we were pleasantly surprised to receive a check for $250 from a lawyer in Florida for a bill incurred long before, which we had no memory of. Let those who doubt the existence of ideals and lament the dishonesty of this materialistic age take note that money is not everything. It is also a reminder to those who grudgingly admit that there are a few honest men but no honest lawyers that even lawyers can possess a sense of honor. There were some interesting escapes during this period. One of my friends lives on the side of Mount Taylor Street, Russia, and has a daughter who lives in Japan and learns wise measures. When the earthquake struck, she immediately poured water into the bathtub. A nearby grocery store, which was doomed, asked customers to help themselves to goods. My friend chose a dozen large siphon bottles of soda water. The house was detached and initially escaped the fire, but eventually, the roof caught fire from flying embers, and the fire began to spread slowly. When it was time to leave the house, a large American flag was raised on a conspicuous staff. A company of soldiers from the Presidio, who were on general duty, saw the flag several blocks away and made their way to the house to save the colors. When water was found in the bathroom, they mixed the toilet with sand and put cast on the burning point. They managed to arrest the spreading flames but could not reach the fire under the cornice. Then they utilized the siphon bottles; one soldier, held by his legs, hung over the roof and squirted the small stream on the crucial spot. The danger was soon over, and the house was saved, along with a group of others that would have burned with it. While many individuals never fully recovered their property or their nerve, it is certain that a new spirit was generated. Great obstacles have been overcome and determination is invincible. We were forced to act broadly, and we reversed the negative policy of doing nothing and owing nothing. We went into debt with our eyes open and spent millions in money for the public good. The city was made safe and beautiful. The City Hall, the Public Library, and the Auditorium make our Civic Center a source of pride. The truly great exposition of 1915 was carried out in a way that increased our courage and our capacity. We have developed a fine public spirit and efficient cooperation. We need fear nothing in the future. We have character and are gaining in capacity. In my entire residence in San Francisco, the occupation and occupation almost evenly allocate my time and energy. I have done some things because I was obliged to and many others because I wished to. When one is fitted and trained for a specific task, they are likely to devote themselves steadily and profitably to it. However, when one is an amateur and not a master, they are sure to be handicapped. About a year after the change of administration in India, I lost my job. For about a year, I worked as a bookkeeper for a stock-broker. Then, for another year, I was a money-broker, selling currency, silver, and revenue stamps. When that business dwindled, I was ready for anything. A friend had loaned money to a printer and seemed about to lose it. In 1867, I became a bookkeeper and assistant in this printing office to rescue the loan, and eventually succeeded. I liked the business and had the courage to buy a small interest, borrowing the necessary money from a bank at one percent a month. I knew very little about the art and even less about business. It meant years of struggling to meet the weekly payroll, often in fear of the sheriff, but I stuck to it and gradually established a good business. I found satisfaction in production and had many pleasant experiences.

Project management is a critical process that involves planning, organizing, and overseeing the various aspects of a project to ensure its successful completion. It requires a high level of expertise in the specific domain the project is focused on. Project managers must be adept at handling all aspects of a project, from inception to completion. One of the key responsibilities of a project manager is to adapt to the internal procedures of the client and establish strong relationships with the nominated representatives. This is essential in ensuring that the project meets its objectives in terms of cost, time, quality, and, most importantly, client satisfaction. There are several key topics that project managers need to focus on, including: 1. Specifying the reason why a project is important and its overall objectives. 2. Defining the quality of the deliverables and the expected outcomes. 3. Estimated project requirements, including projects, materials and finance. 4. Developing a timescale and investment plan for the project. 5. Securing corporate agreement and funding for the project. 6. Implementing a management plan to guide the project team. 7. Building and motivating the project team. 8. Conducting risk assessments and managing changes in the project scope. 9. Monitoring and maintaining the project's progress. 10. Manage the stakeholders, providers and other external parties involved in the project. 11. Closing the project once it has been completed. Project management tools, knowledge and technology are often unique to the field. Some examples include job classification structures, critical path analysis and value-of-benefit management. However, understanding and applying these tools and techniques alone is not sufficient for effective project management. A project manager must possess knowledge and skills from at least four areas of expertise: 1. Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK): A comprehensive guide that outlines the best practices in project management. 2. Application Area Knowledge: Understanding the specific domain or industry the project is focused on. 3. Standards and regulations: familiarization with project management standards and regulations developed by organizations such as the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). 4. General Management Skills: Proficiency in areas such as leadership, communication, and decision-making. 5. Project Environment Management: The ability to manage the project's environment, including its internal and external factors. In summary, effective project management requires a combination of expertise, adaptability, and the use of appropriate tools and techniques. By focusing on the key topics and leveraging their knowledge and skills, project managers can ensure the successful completion of their projects while meeting the objectives and expectations of all stakeholders involved.

This case concerns the debate over the use of the testimony of organizations such as the National Trial Defence Commission on the letterhead of counsel. The court's decision was split, with various justices offering their own perspectives. The plurality opinion did not find justification for banning certifications from legitimate organizations like the NBTA. They believed that the use of such certifications did not inherently mislead the public. Justice Marshall, in his concurring opinion, agreed that the letterhead in question was not misleading in its actual use. However, he noted that the ruling against the use of the NBTA certification should be overturned. He expressed concern that the name “National Trial Defence Council” might lead to a misunderstanding of the organization as a federal body. While most lawyers are aware that the federal government does not regulate lawyers, the general public may not share this knowledge. Justice White, in his dissenting opinion, concurred with Marshall's view that the letterhead could be potentially misleading. However, he disagreed on the approach, stating that it should be the responsibility of the petitioner to clarify their advertisement and remove any potential for misunderstanding. Objections were also raised by Judge O ' Connor, as well as by Judges Renquist and Scalia. They argue that the supervision of lawyers should be left to the Länder in order to have more respect than pluralism permits. The Supreme Court of Illinois, being responsible for monitoring the legal profession within the state, is in a better position to determine which statements may be misleading. In their view, the national courts were the final arbiters to determine whether a declaration was misleading. This case highlights the complexities of professional regulation and the differing views on how to best protect the public from potential misinformation. It underscores the importance of clear communication and transparency in the legal profession.

Jainism, as a religious community, has been a subject of debate regarding its status as a minority in India. In his speech of 3 September 1949, India ' s first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, recognized the existence of various religious minorities, including Jains. He emphasized that India could not be considered a Hindu Rashtra, as it would imply that minorities were not full citizens of the country. The Indian Constitution, in Article 25, guarantees the fundamental right to freedom of religion. Jainism, along with Buddhism and Sikhism, is mentioned in Explanation II of this article, recognizing it as a distinct religion. In a letter dated 31 January 1950, Nehru further assured the Jain delegation that they should not have any concerns about the constitutional position. The second stanza of the Indian National Anthem, "Jana Gana Mana," also acknowledges Jainism as a separate religious denomination, alongside Hinduism, Islam, and other religions. However, the Indian Supreme Court ruled in 2005 that Jains, Sikhs, and Buddhists are part of the broader Hindu fold, as they are Indic religions and interconnected, despite being distinct religions. In 1993, the Committee on National Minorities recommended that the Jain community be declared a minority religious community. This recommendation takes into account the relevant constitutional provisions, the various judicial declarations and the fundamental differences in philosophy between Jainism and other religions. In conclusion, while the status of Jainism in India as a minority religion has been a subject of discussion, it is recognized as a distinct religious community within the Hindu faith community, with its own beliefs and practices.

Curiosity, a fundamental aspect of human nature, is often associated with the desire to learn and understand the world around us. It can be observed in algebra, morality, politics, natural philosophy, etc. This inherent curiosity is not limited to abstract concepts, but extends to the true connection and existence of ideas. In addition to the pursuit of knowledge, there is a distinct curiosity driven by different principles. This form is characterized by an insatiable desire to know about the actions and circumstances of others, even when there is no direct personal interest involved. This type of curiosity often relies on information provided by others, rather than self-directed study or application. In 1954, psychologist Daniel Berlyne further differentiated curiosity into two types: perceptual curiosity and epistemic curiosity. Perceptual curiosity is driven by the need to explore novel stimuli, while epistemic curiosity is the desire to understand and learn new information. In 2004, a psychological measure was developed to assess cognitive and sensory curiosity, thus providing a more detailed understanding of this complex human identity. Intellectual Curiosity in Children Children are naturally curious beings, and their intellectual curiosity can be influenced by the responses they receive from their parents. When parents continue to react negatively to the problems of their children, this may prevent them from asking questions and exploring new ideas, which may stifle their curiosity. Conversely, when parents respond positively to their children's inquiries, it can encourage them to continue asking questions and seeking knowledge, fostering a greater sense of curiosity. Academic performance, intellectual curiosity plays an important role in academic performance. Students who exhibit a strong desire to learn and understand new concepts are more likely to engage with the material, leading to better academic outcomes. Such curiosity can also encourage students to continue their studies, explore new fields of study and promote the overall intellectual development of students.

The arctic mechanism is an ancient Greek analogue computer used to predict astronomical positions and solar eclipses and for computational and astronomic purposes. The origin of cosmic rays remains a mystery a century after their discovery. Supernova remnants (SNRs) are considered potential sources, but whether they can act as cosmic-ray PeVatrons is still uncertain. The connection between cosmic-ray physics and very high-energy (VHE) gamma-ray astronomy is strong, as SNRs should emit VHE gamma rays due to the decay of neutral pions produced in interactions between accelerated cosmic rays and swept-up gas. Evidence for this has been found at GeV energies, and several SNRs are known gamma-ray emitters at TeV energies. However, distinguishing between hadronic and leptonic processes in gamma-ray emission is challenging. Observing SNRs in the >10 TeV energy domain could provide crucial insights, as detection of an SNR spectrum extending to ~100 TeV would indicate hadronic emission and PeVatron status. The proposed key scientific project aims to search for astronomical satellites using the Cherenkov telescope array. The strategy includes deep observations of known sources with hard spectra and hints of multi-TeV spectral extension, as well as searching for diffuse gamma-ray emission around prominent SNRs. The latter is based on the expectation that PeV particles escape the SNR shock and propagate diffusively, producing gamma rays through interactions with ambient gas. SNR RX J1713.7-3946 was the primary target of the survey, as its gamma-ray spectrum showed that the highest energy particles might have escaped. The KSP's scientific objectives are to: 1. Determine the location and manner of accelerating cosmic rays to the energy of the PeV in the Galaxy system. 2. Assessment of whether cosmic rays form a uniform distribution or are concentrated in specific locations. 3. Map the distribution of PeVatrons in the Galaxy. 4. Investigate whether young shell-type SNRs accelerate hadronic cosmic rays to PeV energies. 5. Understand the energy limits and efficiency of this acceleration. The KSP will advance our understanding by: - Exploiting the tight connection between cosmic-ray studies and gamma-ray astronomy, especially the production of gamma rays during cosmic-ray acceleration. - Leveraging CTA's superior sensitivity and spectroscopic capability compared to previous instruments, allowing detection of the most energetic photons and sampling of the highest energy particles in the Galaxy. - Focusing on observations that can resolve the ambiguity between leptonic and hadronic origins at energies above 50 TeV, where the Klein-Nishina effect suppresses leptonic emission. The KSP will specifically observe the sources found in the CTA Galaxy level survey, which will extend to extremely high levels of energy. These observations will measure the spectrum extension, provide precise localization, and identify multi-wavelength counterparts, pinpointing the origin of PeVatrons. The discovery of the most extreme accelerator physics in the galaxy will be a major breakthrough. The project's high-risk/high-gain nature and the importance of developing the Small-Sized Telescope array make it a fitting candidate for a Key Science Project.

The mean number of complexes in the steady state is then easily obtained from this distribution. The technology's enduring legacy is a testament to the ingenuity of its inventor, Fredrik Ljungström, and his contribution to the field of mechanical engineering.

This approach is particularly useful for defining chemical bonds and analyzing the stability of molecular structures. The potential energy, denoted as V, can be expressed as a quadratic form involving the generalized displacement forces (Gq) and a matrix C, which is the compliance matrix. This relationship is given by the following equation: \ [V=frac{]@@2}G_qT C_G\q\quad\text{(eq.) 5)} \] Here, Gq represents the first derivative of the potential energy with respect to the displacement coordinates. This can be expressed as: \\[G_q = H_q QQqud\ text{(eq). In this equation, Hq is a matrix linking displacement forces to the displacement coordinates and Q is the vector representing the displacement coordinates. By replacing Gq expression from equation 6 to equation 5, we obtained an alternative formula for potential energy: \\[V=\frac{%2] TH_qT C H_qQ text\text{(equivalent) 7)} \] This formulation is advantageous because it is independent of the choice of coordinate system and avoids issues with redundant Hessian matrices, which can complicate the calculation of force constants in traditional methods. The compliance matrix C must be positive in order to clearly define potential energy. This means that C is the opposite of the matrix Hq:\[C]=H_q-1]\quad\text{(eq). 8)} \] This relationship ensures that the potential energy is minimized when the system is in its equilibrium state, which corresponds to the lowest energy configuration. The calculation of compliance constants can be applied regardless of the redundancy of the coordinates, making it a versatile tool for analyzing molecular structures. For example, this method can be used to calculate the strength constants of molecules such as cyclobutane, thus understanding the stability and bonding of molecules. In summary, the quadratic form representation of potential energy in terms of generalized displacement forces and the compliance matrix offers a powerful framework for understanding the energetics of molecular systems. This approach is particularly useful for defining chemical bonds and analyzing the stability of molecular structures, as it is coordinate-independent and avoids complications associated with redundant Hessian matrices.

The Extended Hubbard Model (EHM) has been instrumental in elucidating phenomena such as metal-insulator transitions, antiferromagnetism, and high-temperature superconductivity. Despite its simplicity, the EHM encapsulates the fundamental characteristics of strongly correlated electron systems. However, many aspects of the model remain unresolved. In our previous work, we applied the Self-Consistent Random Phase Approximation (SCRPA) to the one-dimensional EHM, demonstrating its effectiveness in treating electron correlations rigorously. Our findings revealed that repulsive off-site interactions enhance conductivity, as evidenced by the vanishing SCRPA energy gap under strong on-site and intermediate off-site repulsions. Yet, the one-dimensional nature of the model precludes any ferromagnetic behavior, limiting its applicability to classical conductors. Driven by the high temperature superconduction found in a cup-like aircraft, the 2D EHM attracted great attention. However, addressing the issue of modalities in general remains challenging. While an exact solution has not been achieved, various approximations have been proposed. Recently, E. Kovacs et al. The four-wheel-drive 4 set of traditional Hubble models provides precise solutions, highlighting the power of shopping and the electronic dynamics described by the field-based response. In this paper, we extend this approach to the EHM, incorporating off-site interactions with interaction energy V. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the model and the computational procedure for constructing an 85x85 Hamiltonian matrix. Section 3 presents our results for ground and gap energies, discussing the impact of off-site interactions on system dynamics. Finally, Section 4 concludes the paper. The two-dimensional EHM on a square lattice is defined by the Hamiltonian: \[ H = -\sum_{\langle i,j \rangle, \sigma} t_{ij} c_{i,\sigma}^{\dagger} c_{j,\sigma} + U\sum_{i} n_{i,\uparrow} n_{i,\downarrow} + V\sum_{\langle i,j \rangle, \sigma, \sigma'} n_{i,\sigma} n_{j,\sigma'} \] This Hamiltonian captures the hopping term \( t \), local repulsion \( U \), and nearest-neighbor repulsion \( V \). For a finite system, the model yields exact solutions for ground state energy, energy gap, and occupation numbers. We consider a 4x4 square lattice at one-eighth filling with periodic boundary conditions, leading to three possible particle configurations and corresponding states. By defining a linear operator \( T \) and leveraging the symmetry properties of the 4x4 cluster, we consolidate the 28800 possible electron distributions into 85 orthogonal cluster states. The Hamiltonian, when applied to the basis vector, results in a non-diagonal r-space basis, necessitating the definition of an 85x85 energy matrix \( E_{nm} \). Numerical determination of eigenvalues and eigenvectors allows for the study of local properties of the lattice. Our results (as shown in figures 2 and 3) show that ground-based energy shows smooth reliance on on field interactions (U \) and linear reliance on off-site interactions (V \). This behavior underscores the role of off-site interactions in shaping the electronic dynamics of the system.

Eye services are an important aspect of Cuba ' s international medical promotion, in particular through the Milagro surgical programme. The initiative focuses on providing eye surgery to patients in Cuba, Venezuela and Latin America, including in Cuba and other countries. As of August 2007, Cuba had performed over 750,000 eye surgeries free of charge, including 113,000 surgeries for its own citizens. The program has since expanded, with 69 Operación Milagro clinics established in 15 countries by 2017. By 2019, the programme had provided free surgery to more than 4 million people in 34 countries. However, there were allegations of programme practice. In South Africa, the 1995 cooperation agreement facilitated the practice of hundreds of Cuban doctors in South Africa. At the same time, South Africa has been sending medical professionals to Cuba to facilitate mutually beneficial exchanges of medical expertise and services.

In this section, we explore the effectiveness of our proposed method through various examples, emphasizing its innovative aspects and contributions. We analyse the different subpopulations within the entire population and distribute the expected results to ensure sustainability, including the expected subpopulations analysed. Utilizing reliability diagrams, we distinguish between the full population (gray points and lines) and the specific subpopulation (black points and lines). Our first example investigates a mixture of subpopulations with a broad range of expected outcomes, except for a narrow gap around specific scores. We select a subpopulation with the highest expected outcome per score, using a rating system that focuses close to zero points. The second example examines a subpopulation with expected outcomes oscillating smoothly between the minimum and maximum values of all subpopulations. The third example analysed the existence of a dispersive subpopulation in the expected outcomes, using a less centralized rating system close to zero. In the fourth example, we use a weighted sample, using the entire population as a subpopulation and with the probability of success with volatility. We have chosen a subpopulation with a unified probability of success and have introduced three outer layers to study its impact on analysis. Remarkably, we observe that heavily weighted observations can lead to misleading results in reliability diagrams, akin to Simpson's Paradox. However, our method of comparing subpopulations via cumulative differences effectively mitigates this issue by subtracting baseline rates, similar to de-trending. Our results demonstrate that while the reliability diagrams and scalar summary statistics capture some aspects of the subpopulation's deviations, they struggle to detect high-frequency oscillations and the impact of heavily weighted observations. On the contrary, despite some random fluctuations, our accumulated deviation plots more accurately reflect the expected results of subpopulations. Furthermore, we analyze the standard training dataset "ImageNet-1000," considering each of the thousand labeled classes as a natural subpopulation. This analysis further confirms that our approach is robust and relevant in real world scenarios. Our innovative approach offers a more nuanced understanding of subpopulation deviations, providing valuable insights for researchers and practitioners alike.

The development of polio vaccines has been a significant milestone in medical history. In the early stages, attempts were made to create a vaccine by using spinal cords from monkeys infected with the polio virus, which were then treated with formaldehyde. One such attempt was made by Dr. Brodie, who first tested the vaccine on himself and his assistants before administering it to three thousand children. Although some children experienced allergic reactions, the vaccine did not confer immunity against polio. In the late 1940s and early 1950s, a major breakthrough was made in the development of polio vaccine, when a research team led by John Anders at the Boston Children's Hospital succeeded in breeding the polio virus in human tissue. This achievement laid the foundation for the creation of effective polio vaccines. Enders, along with his colleagues Thomas H. Weller and Frederick C. Robbins, were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1954 for their groundbreaking work. Two types of polio vaccines are currently used worldwide to combat the disease. The first, developed by Jonas Salk, was tested in 1952 using the HeLa cell line and announced to the public on April 12, 1955. Known as the inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV), it consists of an injected dose of inactivated poliovirus. In 1954, the vaccine underwent extensive field trials, the largest medical experiment in the history of that time. The Protocol was subsequently adopted in 1955 for use by the United States. Following the mass immunization campaign launched by Dimes in March, the number of polio cases declined sharply from nearly 58,000 at the peak to only 5,600 in 1957. Eight years after Sarke ' s achievements, Dr. Albert Sabin developed an alternative polio vaccine known as the oral polio vaccine. The vaccine uses an verbable but weakened form of the polio virus. The development of these vaccines has played a crucial role in the global effort to eradicate polio.

For several reasons, the concept of overloading of vaccines was considered to be biologically untrustworthy. Firstly, both vaccinated and unvaccinated children exhibit similar immune responses to infections unrelated to vaccines. Secondly, autism is not classified as an immune-mediated disease. Consequently, the notion that vaccines could trigger autism by overwhelming the immune system contradicts the current understanding of autism's pathogenesis. As a result, the hypothesis that vaccines cause autism has been largely discredited by the preponderance of scientific evidence. Regarding prenatal infections, research has established a correlation between schizophrenia and exposure to certain infections during pregnancy, such as rubella, influenza, and toxoplasmosis. For instance, one study reported a sevenfold increase in the risk of schizophrenia when mothers were infected with influenza during the first trimester of pregnancy. This finding has a significant impact on public health, as measures to prevent infection include vaccinations, good hygiene and the use of antibiotics in cases of poisoning. In animal models, theoretical concerns have been raised about the potential link between schizophrenia and the maternal immunisation response induced by antigens. A 2009 review concluded that there was inadequate evidence to endorse the routine use of the trivalent influenza vaccine during the first trimester of pregnancy. However, vaccines are still recommended for use outside the first three months and in specific circumstances, such as women during epidemics or certain sanitary conditions. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention ' s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and the United States College of Gynaecologists and Gynaecologists provided guidelines for vaccination during pregnancy to ensure the health and safety of mothers and developing foetuses. It is crucial to follow these recommendations to minimize the risk of prenatal infections and their potential consequences.

In this paper, we explore the use of auxiliary inputs to address the challenges of partial observability in reinforcement learning (RL). Our main contributions include the introduction of new complementary inputs and comprehensive experimental analyses to demonstrate their effectiveness. In particular, we propose to use future projections, general value functions and predictive national representations to enhance learning in a partially observable environment. We also suggest combining different forms of auxiliary inputs to capture both past and future information, as well as using them to improve exploration strategies. Our experimental setup involves the Lobster Fishing environment, a partially observable Markov decision process (MDP) where an agent must collect rewards while dealing with stochastic transitions and reward regeneration. We have detailed observations of vectors, random sources and multi-purpose drive structures in figure ref{fig:lobster_mdp}. Our experiments utilize the Sarsa(0) learning algorithm with linear function approximation and Adam optimizer, sweeping over various hyperparameters to identify the best performing configurations. We compare the performance of agents using auxiliary inputs against two baselines: an observations-only agent and an optimal agent with full knowledge of the environment's dynamics. Observation agents are used only as benchmarks for supporting input impacts, while the best agents provide a ceiling on achievable performance. We introduce two main types of auxiliary inputs for the Lobster environment: exponential decaying traces and particle filtering. Decay marks capture the history of reward collection, while particle filtering provides a general state of belief based on particle weight. Both methods are integrated into the agent's state representation, allowing the agent to learn a policy that considers additional context beyond the immediate observation. Our results in figure ref{fig:lobster_pf_slavilihood_3d} show that agents using auxiliary inputs can achieve performance closer to the best media and rely solely on the observation baseline. This demonstrates the potential of auxiliary inputs to mitigate the challenges of partial observability in RL. Finally, our work emphasizes the importance of considering complementary inputs in labour contracts, especially in complex and partially visible environments. By integrating more information into the learning process, agencies can develop stronger policies that take into account uncertainty and improve overall performance. Future research directions include exploring more advanced complementary inputs and investigating their implications for exploration and for summing up during research days.

In the fields of telecommunications, computer networking, and programming, the term "timeout" or "time-out" encompasses a variety of concepts. It generally refers to network parameters that activate an event after the prescribed time has passed. The timeout mechanism is designed to enhance the efficient use of limited resources and prevent indefinite waiting for certain actions or responses. Overtime can be defined as a predetermined period within which the system will await a specific event. If an incident does not occur within the specified time frame, the system will initiate pre-determined action. Importantly, a timeout condition can be canceled if an appropriate timeout cancellation signal is received. Timeouts are critical in situations where systems need to wait for action or response. By setting a timeout, the system avoids indefinite waiting, which can be inefficient and wasteful of resources. Instead, the system takes predetermined action after the expiration of the period, assuming that further waiting is futile and that different courses of action are required. Several examples illustrate the application of timeouts in different contexts: 1. In the Microsoft Windows and ReactOS command-line interfaces, the "timeout" command is used to pause the command processor for a specified number of seconds. This allows for a temporary halt in the execution of subsequent commands. 2. In Post Office Protocol (POP) connections, the server typically closes the connection if it remains idle for a certain period. This time-out mechanism ensures that resources are not wasted on idle connections, but is available to other users or missions. Timeouts play a vital role in optimizing system performance and resource allocation. By setting reasonable time frames, systems can manage their resources effectively and respond appropriately to situations, thereby strengthening overall functionality and user experience.

This section introduces a novel approach for constructing a Pickands function that can be flexibly fitted to data. Our method offers a highly-parameterized approximation that adheres to the constraints of a Pickands function while remaining computationally feasible. The structure of this paper is as follows: a review of past extreme value plastics (EVC) modelling methods, followed by a detailed explanation of our methods and a discussion of theoretical and practical aspects. Subsequent sections include modelling studies and practical data applications, concluding with a discussion of methodological performance and possible future work. In the relevant work, we discussed the classification of the EVC model approach into non-parameters and parameter estimations. Non-parametric models have greater flexibility, especially for asymmetric data, although they vary considerably. Parametric models perform well in higher dimensions with mild asymmetry, especially when utilizing Khoudraji's asymmetric extension. We have highlighted the limitations of the existing methodology and have proposed a semi-parameter approach using the sample, inspired by recent progress on the ground. Our method involves a geometric transformation that simplifies the modeling of a Pickands function by converting it into a 2-monotone function. This transformation is achieved through an affine transformation, which maps the support lines of the Pickands function onto a new coordinate system. The resulting 2-monotone function is easier to model and can be derived from the Pickands function using a one-to-one correspondence. This approach has made the presentation of the Pickands function more flexible and accurate and overcomes the limitations of the existing methodology. The innovative aspects of our research include the development of a new semiparametric EVC model, the use of splines for Pickands function approximation, and the application of the Williamson transform to model an Archimedean generator. Our contribution is aimed at providing a more basic sound and universal building for the polarized EVC families, especially in the context of asymmetric treatment.

In electric engines, short circuits between general appliances and brushes may cause a number of problems. When power is produced at hundreds of watts, this short power can cause severe heat heat heaters, brushes and metal brushes, which can cause air ventilator brushes to be welded. It is important to note that carbon brushes are not commonly used for welding. Such short circuits are extremely inefficient, as they quickly empty batteries and require much higher power supply components than are required for engines to operate without short circuits. To mitigate this problem, one solution is to introduce a gap between the commutator plates that is wider than the ends of the brushes. This approach not only eliminates the shorting issue but also increases the zero-torque range of angular positions. When an engine begins to rotate with external force, it continues to rotate. Additionally, it can be effectively turned off by stalling it in a position within the zero-torque angle range, where the commutator is not in contact with the brushes. This design is sometimes utilized in homebuilt hobby motors, such as those created for science fairs, and can be found in some published science project books. However, there is a clear downside to this simple solution. Engines now go through two revolutions of large-scale rotation of arcs to the coast. While this may be suitable for applications like electric fans or maintaining the spin of a flywheel, it is not adequate for many other uses. For instance, it would be unsuitable for driving the capstan of a tape transport or any similar application where continuous, uninterrupted torque is required.

The Tsunami Joint Development Programme Protocol is a high-speed document transfer agreement that operates through a network path with high bandwidth and durable products. It is specifically designed to address the limitations of the standard TCP protocol, which is often efficient under the conditions of such a network. The Tsunami protocol was created at the Advanced Network Management Laboratory of Indiana University. The agreement facilitates the transmission of documents by dividing them into a series of numbered blocks of approximately 32 kbps each. This method allows for efficient data transmission by optimizing the use of the available bandwidth. Communication between the client and server is managed through a low-bandwidth TCP connection, which is used to coordinate the transfer process. On the contrary, bulk data are themselves transmitted through UDP, thus taking advantage of its ability to process a large amount of data quickly. The combination of TCP for control communication and UDP for data transfer makes the Tsunami UDP Protocol a versatile solution for high-speed file transfers in challenging network environments. This approach is particularly useful in situations where bandwidth delay products are of significant importance, for example in long-distance or satellite networks. For more information and resources related to the Tsunami UDP Protocol, interested readers can refer to the project's page on SourceForge, which provides additional details, documentation, and community support.

In this study, we have explored the new area of zero-knowledge zero-throat learning, which represents a significant advance in universal zero-throat learning and open identification. The ZK-ZSL paradigm is designed to identify categories within source data sets and to identify new and invisible categories without any prior knowledge, while re-establishing their semantic attributes. The study addressed two main challenges for ZK-ZSL: the need to distinguish between intangible entities without previous labels and the absence of semantic labels for implicit categories, which could lead to biased projections. Our approach has innovatively restored the observed and invisible cluster structure of the categories where the target data are concentrated, using source labels to guide the approximation of the categories observed. We introduce a unique structural alignment loss that enhances the semantic understanding of unseen categories based on their recovered clustering structures. Through comprehensive experiments on four benchmark datasets, our method demonstrates superior performance in classification accuracy and semantic recovery, validating the effectiveness of our novel contributions. To further validate our approach, we conducted a hyperparameter analysis on the AWA2 dataset, examining the impact of varying the prediction loss and structural alignment loss parameters, $\alpha$ and $\beta$. We found that when both parameters were set at 1.0, the accuracy of the optimal classification and semantic recovery was achieved, highlighting the robustness of our default parameter configuration. The analysis revealed a reverse U-type relationship between parameters and performance measures, indicating that our approach managed a sensitive balance very well. In conclusion, our work presents a pioneering solution in the field of visual recognition, pushing the boundaries of what is achievable in zero-shot learning scenarios. The innovative aspects of our research, including the structural alignment loss and the method's adaptability to unseen categories, contribute significantly to the advancement of knowledge in this domain.
