Other causes of pain in an enlarged liver include: - Traction of the supporting ligaments when standing or walking - The liver pressing against the rib cage or pinching the abdominal wall - Straining the lumbar spine - In some postures, the liver may pinch the parietal peritoneum against the lower rib cage, resulting in sharp, transient pain that is relieved by changing position Additionally, a tumor may infiltrate the liver's capsule, causing dull or occasionally stabbing pain. In contrast, kidney and spleen cancers tend to be less painful than liver tumours. Kidney tumors typically cause pain only when the organ has been significantly affected. It is important to note that the information provided here is of a general nature and may not be applicable in each individual case. Diagnosis and treatment should always be based on a thorough medical assessment by qualified health professionals.

This section presents methods that approximate the multivariant probabilistic density function, which is essential to the high-dimensional space-efficient Bayes inference. We begin with the estimation of Gaussian distributions, where a full covariance matrix is employed for dimensions up to four, and a diagonal covariance matrix is used for higher dimensions, scaled by a factor derived from the normal reference rule. For the mixture model, we propose the use of the Gaussian mixture, whose parameters are determined by the expected maximization and the selection of the number of components according to the Bayes information standard. In scenarios where the prior distribution is bounded, we introduce truncated Gaussian mixtures that incorporate known bounds within the mixture components. We also explore the use of vine copulas to decompose multivariate distributions into marginal distributions and a copula function that captures dependency structures. The optimal copula function is chosen by minimizing the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), and the vine structure is determined using a maximum spanning tree with Kendall's tau edge weights. In terms of marginal distributions, we consider empirical distribution functions, Pareto tails to enhance accuracy in the tails, and parametric mixtures for both unbounded and bounded variables. These distribution parameters were estimated using the expected maximum and the number of components selected for the individual classification was minimized. For estimates of density based on returns, we use the Gaussian process to return, which is flexible and naturally deals with variable returns. The Gaussian process is gradually integrating into one by calculating its overall nature and adjusting a normal constant. We experiment with two covariance functions, the squared exponential and the Matérn kernel with ν=3/2, optimizing the length scale parameter through cross-validation. Finally, we discussed the use of a major re-assessment, using the initial Monte Carlo sample for direct re-evaluation as a reference for the approximate methodology presented. This approach emphasizes the innovative aspects of our research, providing a comprehensive toolkit for approximating multivariate probability density functions in Bayesian inference.

Fibre-optic communications have revolutionized the telecommunications sector, providing high-speed data transmission with minimal signal losses. Technology demonstrated its potential for the first time in long beaches in California, where 6 million bits/seconds are transported by fibre-optics. This breakthrough paved the way for the widespread introduction of fibre optics into the telecommunications network. One of the earliest wide area network fiber optic cable systems was installed by Rediffusion in Hastings, East Sussex, UK, in 1978. The system serves more than 1,000 users, using cables laid throughout the town. At that time, the main purpose of the cables was to transmit television channels that could not be provided because of local reception problems. The first trans-Atlantic telephone cable using fibre-optic technology is TAT-8, which is based on the best laser magnification technology in Survire. This pioneering cable was launched in 1988, further consolidating the role of fibre-optics in global telecommunications. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, industrial promoters and research companies such as KMI and RHK predicted a significant increase in demand for telecommunications bandwidth. This surge is due to the growing popularity of the Internet and the commercialization of bandwidth-intensive consumer services, such as demand video. The exponential growth of Internet protocol (IP) data flows has exceeded the increase in the complexity of integrated circuits as described in Moore ' s law. Understanding the essential elements of a telecommunications system is essential to master the full impact of fibre optics. The transmitter, also known as the source of information, is responsible for converting information into signal transmission. In electronic and telecommunications terms, transmitters or radio transmitters are electronic devices that generate radio waves with the help of antennas. These radio waves are essential for broadcasting and are a vital component of many electronic devices that communicate wirelessly. The integration of fiber optics into telecommunication systems has significantly enhanced data transmission capabilities, enabling faster and more reliable communication across vast distances. As technology evolves, the role of fibre-optics in telecommunications is expected to increase, further shaping the way we connect and share information in the digital age.

Possession of placenta, i.e. white language disease, can be influenced by spiritual and practical factors. In some cultures, such as in Saudi Arabia, traditional practices to honor the placenta may include burial rather than consumption. These practices often involve waiting to sever the umbilical cord until it stops pulsing, which helps prevent blood loss and infection, and maintaining the placental connection until after delivery and the onset of nursing. Although modern placenta practices are relatively rare in contemporary human culture, 2012 was a cause for some concern, with American actress Parlio Jones claiming that eating placenta helped her return to work quickly after giving birth. Some modern societies have documented examples of placenta malformations. In the 1960s, for example, a medical official in Czechoslovakia reported that nurses in Viet Nam and midwives of Chinese and Thai nationality had consumed placenta for young, healthy patients for unknown reasons. The placentas were prepared by removing the membranous parts and frying them with onions before consumption. Researchers at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, carried out an intercultural and ethnographic study, surveyed 179 contemporary human societies and identified examples of foetal malformations. The study highlighted cultural diversity in the practice of birth and the different ways in which placenta is treated and respected in different societies. It is important to note that while some individuals may choose to consume the placenta for personal or cultural reasons, the scientific evidence supporting the health benefits of placentophagy remains limited and inconclusive.

In this paper, we have explored the definition of disturbance of scattering amplitude, which has traditionally been rooted in quantum field theory and is characterized by Feynman's spine and graphs. We explore an alternative paradigm where amplitudes are fundamental, with the $S$-matrix constructed from a minimal set of data and rules, termed a "diagrammar." Our approach hinges on defining the $S$-matrix through its singularities, a concept that has remained a vibrant and productive area of research. Our central contribution is the construction of an $S$-matrix for a theory of Einstein gravity, augmented by $R^3$ terms, using the singularity structure of three-point amplitudes. We operate within a non-quality theory, using distorted variables to express an amplitude with a clearly defined “carat weight.” We use Einstein's three-point standard amplitude to present our theory and expand it by incorporating another three-point amplitudes that have a higher power in an instant. These extensions are not triple and must depend entirely on $\spa{i}.j$ or $\spb{i}.j$. The key to our approach is to require that the amplitude show the correct symmetry and uniqueness. We demonstrate that the entire $S$-matrix can be determined from these vertices if we enforce the amplitudes to factorize on simple poles. This factor has been shaped by two key shifts: the original British-Cacaso-Fen-Vitten (BCFW) shift and the shift in spreads. Both transformations translate instantaneously into complex variables of z, while maintaining full conditions and overall momentum. We focus on the leading $\alpha$ contribution to the $S$-matrix, examining both four-point and five-point amplitudes. For the four-point amplitude, we found that all the amplitudes were not zero and the correct symmetry was shown when the appropriate conversions were used. Conversely, the single minus amplitude necessitates the BCFW shift. For the five-point amplitudes, we achieve an all-plus amplitude that maintains full crossing symmetry and is independent of an arbitrary spinor. Our results not only align with previous computations using field theory methods but also resonate with the UV infinite pieces of gravity in various dimensions. This work highlights the strength of the shell-cycle approach in determining scattering amplitudes and provides a new perspective for constructing the dollar-S$ matrix from the minimum amplitude group.

Leprosy, also known as leprosy, is a chronic infectious disease caused by bacterial Mycobacterium leprae. It mainly affects the upper respiratory tract ' s skin, peripheral nerves, respiratory tracts and muscle surfaces. Early diagnosis and multi-drug treatment treatment are essential to prevent complications such as neurological injuries and disabilities. In Indonesia, the prevalence rate of leprosy in the 21st century is slightly under one new case per 10,000 people, with approximately 20,000 new cases detected each year. However, the rate is significantly higher in certain regions, particularly South Sulawesi, where there are more than three new cases per 10,000 people, and North Maluku, with more than five new cases per 10,000 people. The Indonesian government provides MDT free of charge to patients who require it. Some hospitals in major population centres are designed to meet the medical needs of those affected by the disease. Despite improvements in early detection and treatment, about 10 per cent of patients in Indonesia have suffered significant neurological or other damage before they discovered and treated their disease. This is often due to a lack of awareness and widespread stigma associated with leprosy, which deters people living with leprosy from seeking treatment. To combat this stigma and eliminate discrimination against people with leprosy, PERMATA (Perhimpunan Mandiri Kusta) Indonesia was established in 2007. The organization was founded by a group of individuals who had all been treated for leprosy. They worked to establish connections with key figures among those with the disease in communities in South Sulawesi, East Java, and NTT—three provinces with some of the highest incidence rates of leprosy in the country. Efforts to raise awareness, educate the public and support people affected by leprosy are essential to reduce the impact of the disease in Indonesia. By addressing the social and medical challenges associated with leprosy, the country can work towards a future where no one suffers from the consequences of this ancient and curable disease.

High-power radio frequency devices play a key role in applications such as industrial radio frequency heating, particle accelerators and radio transmitters. This is particularly important in microwave frequencies, where devices such as GHz and mobile bellows are used to magnify the level of power that is not currently available with semiconductor equipment. Home microwaves are a common example of a device that produces microwave power effectively, producing hundreds of watts using magnet tubes. While solid-state devices made of materials such as nitrification are promising as possible alternatives, they are still at an early stage of development and are quite expensive. In military applications, high-power vacuum tubes can generate signals in the range of 10 to 100 megawatts, which can potentially damage an unprotected receiver's frontend. These devices, classified as non-nuclear electromagnetic weapons, were first introduced by the United States and Russia in the late 1990s. In the music industry, tube magnifiers remain commercially viable in specific locations. They are highly valued for their warm sound, their over-drive performance and their ability to replicate the properties of the tube recordings of previous times. This makes these works very popular in sound information equipment, instruments amplifiers and devices used in studios. Many guitarists prefer valve magnifiers, not solid models, because they're distorted when they're too driven. It is important to note that any amplifier can only accurately zoom the signal into a certain volume. Beyond this limit, the amplifier will begin to distort the signal. Different circuits will cause varying degrees and types of distortion, which can be a desirable feature for some musicians.

The golden ratio, often denoted by the Greek letter φ (phi), is a mathematical constant that has intrigued mathematicians and artists for centuries. It is defined as the ratio of two quantities where the sum of the quantities and the larger quantity are equal, expressed as φ = a/b. This ratio is approximately 1.618033988749895. The golden angle, a concept closely related to the golden ratio, is the angle subtended at the center of a circle by an arc that is a fraction of the circle's circumference. This score is given by the equivalent of the gold ratio, which is expressed as f = b/ (a+b) = 1/ (1). Since 1 + φ equals φ squared (φ^2), the fraction f simplifies to 1/φ^2. This implies that φ^2 golden angles can fit within a full circle. The numerical value of the golden angle can be approximated by multiplying the fraction f by the full angle of a circle, which is 360 degrees or 2π radians. Thus, the gold cornerg can be calculated as follows: - degrees: g 360 x 0.38 1966 x 137.50778° - radians: g 2 x 0.38 1966 x 2.39996 radians. Gold horns have a fascinating presence in nature, particularly in pollen, which is a study of the stratification of trunk leaves. One well-known example is the pattern of florets on a sunflower, where the angle between adjacent florets is closely related to the golden angle. It is believed that this arrangement will maximize the packaging density of the oil slick and optimize the distribution of sunlight and resources. The importance of golden horns in nature has been the subject of mathematical models, suggesting that the patterns observed in sunflowers and other plants may spontaneously result from solutions to the non-linear partial differential equations on the plane. This shows the deep connection between mathematics and nature, highlighting golden horns as a key element in the complex patterns found in nature.

In this section, we delve into the intricate details of our research, which revolves around the mathematical constructs of algebraic curves and their associated fields. We first adopt an innovative approach to understanding the multi-modal structures in these areas, which we call $F-ast. Our methodology hinges on the concept of a 'factorized form', which allows us to express every element $f$ in $F^{\ast}$ as a product of simpler components, each associated with a pair of points on the curve. This factorization is underpinned by a set of multiplicative constants, which we carefully select to ensure consistency across the entire curve. Then we put forward a proposal to formalize our approach, showing that it is indeed possible to select these constants in a manner that meets our multiplier formula for each element of the dollar. The evidence for this assertion is based on the algebra structure of the curve and its related fields and draws on principles such as the Well Reciprocal Law. Our research also explores the concept of ideles, which are elements of a field that exhibit specific multiplicative properties. We introduce a family of ideles that possess a unique property, allowing them to be expressed in terms of the logarithmic difference of their components. This family of ideles serves as an algebraic analogue to the classical Schottky-Klein prime form, a multi-valued function with a rich history in complex analysis. In the realm of genus zero curves, we provide explicit expressions for our ideles and the associated constants, offering a concrete example of our abstract concepts. We also define algebraic analogs of multiplicative multi-valued functions, which are key to understanding the structure of the fields associated with algebraic curves. Our research culminates in the introduction of local quantum field theories, which are mathematical models that describe physical phenomena at a local level. In our view, there are three different types of theory, each corresponding to different algebra structures: the Heisenberg algebra, the algebra and the central extension of the multiplying group using stationery symbols. The Heisenberg Lie algebra, a central extension of the geometric loop algebra, is a cornerstone of our local quantum field theories. We define this algebra and its associated modules, which are key to understanding the algebraic structure of our fields. Our definition is based on a continuous double-line format, which is an essential aspect of the field algebra structure. In summary, our research offers a novel perspective on the algebraic structure of fields associated with algebraic curves, introducing new concepts and methodologies that have the potential to enrich our understanding of these mathematical constructs. Our work is characterized by a blend of abstract algebraic theory and concrete examples, providing a comprehensive exploration of the topic.

A needle-point is an ancient Chinese medical practice whose rich history is rooted in various faith systems around celestial bodies and bodies. These systems believed that certain elements aligned at specific times, influencing the effectiveness of acupuncture treatments. Endeham and Lu, the time contestants, describe these “arbitrary predictions” in complex graphics and specialized terms (Needham and Lu, 140-41). During this period, needle needles are much thicker than modern needles, often leading to infection. Contrary to the contemporary understanding of sterilization, it was commonly believed that infections were caused by using the wrong needle, needling at the wrong location, or at an inopportune time (Needham and Lu, 102–03). In response to this situation, needles are sometimes heated in boiling water or fire, and needles are used at injection points during heat, resulting in scalding effects (Needham and Lu, 104). The Great Compendium of Acupuncture and Moxibustion, published in 1601, recommended the use of nine needles. This figure may be influenced by ancient Chinese beliefs about nine kinds of magic (Needham and Lu, 102-03). Other faith systems assume that the human body operates on a rhythmal basis and that needle pricks need to be carried out at the right point of the rhythm in order to achieve the best results (Needham and Lu, 140-41). Imbalances between Yin and Yang were also considered a potential cause of disease in some belief systems (Needham and Lu, 140–41). The First Century Anti-Dumping Agreement marked an important period of acupuncture development, as the first books on the issue had been published and the emergence of recognized acupuncture experts had begun. These early texts, which included Zhou Jiu Jian Jianjin, were published in the middle of the third century.

High Dynamic Area Imaging (HDRI) is a technique used to capture and display a wider light intensity than conventional imaging systems. This technology is particularly useful in scenarios where the contrast between the brightest and darkest areas is significant, such as in outdoor photography or computer graphics. The development of the Human Development Report in computer graphics is closely linked to advances in sunglasses technology, which is a small program that determines how graphics are made available on screen. The evolution of the masked model has played a crucial role in shaping high-powered wave-band images. The initial release of Shader Model 1.0 with DirectX 8 in the early 2000s introduced standard lighting, which illuminated 3D worlds. However, this method had limitations. The lighting precision was confined to 8-bit integers, which restricted the contrast ratio to 256:1. This meant that the brightest white was only 255 levels brighter than the darkest shade above pure black. Additionally, lighting calculations were based on integers, which did not accurately represent the real world, where light intensities can vary infinitely. On 24 December 2002, Microsoft released DirectX 9.0, which includes Shader Model 2.0. This update was a significant step towards enabling the rendering of high-dynamic-range images. Shader Model 2.0 allowed for lighting precision beyond the 8-bit limitation, with programmers having the option to use up to 24 bits for lighting precision. While the calculations are still largely based on integer numbers, the increased accuracy reflects more accurately the lighting of 3D scenarios. One of the first graphics cards to support DirectX 9.0 natively was ATI's Radeon 9700. However, it took a few years for a game developer to take full advantage of the Shader 2.0 model's ability to play in the game. On 23 August 2003, Microsoft further updated versions DirectX to 9.0b, which introduced pixel shadow 2.x. This update further enhanced the capabilities of shader technology, paving the way for more advanced rendering techniques and a more realistic representation of high-dynamic-range images in computer graphics.

Digital twins, as virtual replicas of physical entities, are revolutionizing various sectors by offering real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and optimization. This paper explores the application of digital twins in education, smart cities, transportation, energy, and other industries, highlighting their potential to transform traditional practices. In the field of education, digital twins can provide personalized learning experiences using AI-driven robotic and adaptive learning frameworks. They can help bridge the gap between industrial needs and academic courses and promote targeted human development. For instance, Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) can benefit from AI-powered personalization, enhancing the effectiveness of teaching and learning. In the context of smart cities, digital twins can engage citizens in city planning, optimize energy consumption, and improve transportation systems. They can also enable real-time monitoring and control of urban infrastructure, enhancing sustainability and efficiency. Smart grids, for example, can leverage digital twins for dynamic power usage management and predictive maintenance. Our research introduces an innovative approach to digital twin development, focusing on five key enabling technologies: physics-based modeling, data-driven modeling, big data cybernetics, infrastructure and platforms, and human-machine interfaces. Physics-based modeling, despite its limitations, remains a cornerstone of digital twin development, offering a foundation for understanding physical phenomena. Our approach combines experimental and numerical modeling techniques to create accurate and reliable digital twins. Data-driven modeling, on the other hand, leverages machine learning and AI algorithms to analyze large datasets, enabling predictive analytics and decision-making. This approach complements physics-based modeling, providing insights into complex systems that are difficult to model using traditional methods. Big data network theory is another key component of our approach to data security, management and quality challenges. By using the power of big data, we can develop more accurate and powerful digital twins that can adapt to changing conditions and circumstances. Infrastructure and platforms are essential to support the development and deployment of digital twins. Our research explores the use of cloud computing, IoT, and other technologies to create scalable and flexible digital twin platforms that can cater to diverse application needs. Finally, human-machine interfaces play a crucial role in ensuring the usability and accessibility of digital twins. Our approach focuses on the development of intuition and interactive interfaces to facilitate seamless interaction between users and digital twins, and to enhance user experience and decision-making. Finally, our research proposes a comprehensive and innovative digital two-way approach to development that addresses common challenges, uses enabling technologies and creates far-reaching solutions in various sectors. By combining physics-based modeling, data-driven modeling, big data cybernetics, infrastructure and platforms, and human-machine interfaces, we can unlock the full potential of digital twins and drive the digital transformation of industries.

Taste is a complex sensory experience that is influenced by various factors. The flavor of a food product is determined not only by the natural aromas present in the ingredients and added flavorings, but also by accompanying substances such as flavor enhancers, sweeteners, acidulants, and salt substitutes. Polyols, like sorbitol and maltitol, serve as carriers in flavorings and also contribute a sweet taste to the product. Interestingly, the color of food can significantly impact the perception of taste. One study found that the addition of more red to the beverage increased its perceived sweetness, and although the concentration of Sougros was low, dark-colour solutions were 2-10 per cent higher than light solutions. Food manufacturers often take advantage of this phenomenon, as can be seen from the different colours of products such as Frost Loops cereals and Gummy Bears, which often use the same taste. Flavor enhancers, also known as taste enhancers, are umami or "savory" compounds that intensify the taste of food without being flavorings themselves. They are mainly based on amino acid and nucleic acid, which are commonly used as sodium or calcium salt. The European Union recognizes and approves certain tomato spices. In Europe, under EU legislation, substances that are entirely sweet, acid or salty are not regarded as spices (article 2 of Regulation (EC) No. 1334/2008). In addition, according to EU legislation, spice auxiliaries are classified as additives rather than spices (point 14 of annex I to Regulation (EC) No. 1333/2008). This distinction is important for the regulation and labeling of food products in the European market.

\section{Synthetic Data Experiment} Our synthetic data experiment is designed to analyse the performance of the \textsc{Memorize} method that we propose under controlled conditions, using measurements and baselines that are not available in real data sets. We use two key metrics to evaluate \textsc{memoreze}: remember probability and forget ratio at the point of the future. These metrics allow us to assess both long-term and short-term retention by adjusting the value of $\tau$. We compare \textsc{Memorize} with three baselines: uniform, last-minute, and threshold-based reviewing schedules. The results described in figure ref{fig:synthetic_one_card} show that \textsc{memorize} is consistently higher than the baseline in terms of two quality measures. It also shows greater robustness across runs and reduces reviewing intensity over time as recall probability improves. In addition, we investigate the impact of the learning effort parameter, which controls the number of review activities required. Lower values of $q$ lead to quicker memorization, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:learning-effort}. Furthermore, we explore the effects of learner aptitude and item difficulty, represented by parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Higher values of $\alpha$ and lower values of $\beta$ indicate quicker memorization. Figure~\ref{fig:aptitude-learner} illustrates how these parameters influence the time taken to reach a specific forgetting rate. \subsection{Experiments on Real Data} In this section, we evaluate the effectiveness of different reviewing schedules using real data from Duolingo, a popular language-learning platform. Our goal is to assess how well each schedule spaces reviews. Due to the inability to intervene in real datasets, we rely on likelihood comparisons to determine how closely a (user, item) pair followed a particular reviewing schedule. We use a data set of about 12 million classes, involving 5.3 million unique (user, word) classes. After pre-treatment, our data sets consist of about 5.2 million unique pairs. Half-life regression and maximum probability estimates are used to estimate model parameters. We then compute the likelihood of reviewing events for each (user, item) pair under different reviewing schedules. Our methodology allows us to determine how closely a (user, item) pair follows a particular reviewing schedule, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:sample_trace}. Since it is not possible to make a repercussional probability measure in the future, we have focused on alternative quality measures that do not depend on the choice of memory models.

When food is mixed with foreign substances, food contamination occurs, which can occur at various stages of the food production chain, including production, transport, packaging, storage, marketing and cooking. Pollution can take different forms, such as physical, chemical or biological contamination. Physical contamination, also known as the presence of foreign bodies, involves objects such as hair, plant branches, plastic fragments or metals. When such an object enters food, it is considered to be a physical contaminant. If these foreign objects carry bacteria, they can cause physical and biological contamination. Common sources of physical pollution include hair, glass, metals, pests, jewellery, mud and nails. Material food contamination is a dangerous event that can lead to negative consequences. It is natural, though unexpected, that food is contaminated during preparation by hazardous items found in kitchens or production facilities. Insanitary conditions in these areas increase the likelihood of physical contamination. The consumption of food containing physical pollutants may pose a number of risks to individuals, including asphyxiation, tooth damage and internal injuries. Children and older persons are particularly vulnerable to the harmful effects of food pollution, as their immune systems are weak and their physical structures are fragile. One of the main causes of physical contamination is the removal of food, the absence of lids and exposure to potential contaminants. In order to prevent such pollution and protect consumers from harm, adequate hygiene and hygiene standards must be maintained in food-preparation zones, particularly in restaurants and other food services.

Interoperability is a critical concept that refers to the ability of different systems, units, or organizations to work together seamlessly. The concept is not limited to physical components but extends to the interface between organizations and systems, particularly in the areas of communications and computer technology. At the technical level, interoperability is essential to ensure that systems have the necessary technical capacity to work in a coordinated manner. This is particularly important in the context of mission compatibility, where the seamless integration of systems and data is essential for the success of coalition partners. One of the key benefits of technological interoperability is its impact on operational and tactical levels. It enhances flexibility by allowing for more effective communication and coordination between the different entities. This is particularly important in situations where rapid response and decision-making are required. Public security is another area where interoperability plays a key role. First responders, such as law enforcement, firefighting, emergency medical services, and other public health and safety departments, need to be able to communicate effectively during wide-scale emergencies. Inadequate interoperability can hamper the exchange of key information, lead to delays in response and may undermine public safety. Over the past 12 years, significant investments and research have been made in the field of interoperability, particularly in the public safety sector. However, differences and incompatibility in hardware pose challenges to seamless communication between different agencies. Information systems such as computer-assisted delivery systems and records management systems often operate in isolation, creating so-called “islands of information.” To fill these gaps, agencies have introduced inefficient ad hoc solutions. Large agencies have also begun to implement limited interoperable systems, but these methods have proved inadequate. The importance of public safety interoperability was emphasized in the 9/11 attacks on the Pentagon and the World Trade Centre, and the lack of interoperability was a major problem. This highlights the need for improved communication and coordination among agencies and systems. Further evidence of the challenges posed by a lack of interoperability has emerged in various incidents, emphasizing the need for continued efforts to improve the integration and compatibility of systems across different organizations and sectors. As technology evolves, the importance of ensuring that systems can work together effectively will only increase, making interoperability an important aspect of modern communication and coordination.

In 1901, it was found that high doses of radiation could harm people. The French physicist Henry Bakerquell carried out an experiment with a radioactive sample in his pocket. This leads to a high local dose of radiation, which causes radiation to burn. This incident led to further investigation into the biological properties of radiation, which eventually contributed to the development of medical treatments. Ernest Rutherford, working in Canada and England, made significant contributions to the understanding of radioactive decay. He designed a simple equation, now known as one-step kinetic energy, to describe the process. This equation revealed that a given radioactive substance has a characteristic "half-life," which is the time taken for the radioactivity present in a source to decrease by half. Rutherford has also introduced the terminology Alpha, Beta and gamma rays to classify different types of radiation. He converted nitrogen into oxygen through a series of experiments. Most notably, he supervised the students who conducted the Geiger-Marsden experiment, also known as the Geiger-Marsden experiment. This experiment overthrew the “budding model” of the atom proposed by J.J. Thomson in 1904. The plum pudding model shows that the atom is made of a cluster of positive cloud-enclosed electrons to balance the electrone charge. However, experiments on copper and copper in gold show that the positive charge is concentrated in a very small core. This finding led to the development of the Rutherford atomic model, which was subsequently improved by the Bol model. In the Bor model, the positive core is surrounded by negative charge electrons. In 1934, Irène Joliot-Curie, daughter of Marie Curie, and her husband Frédéric Joliot-Curie continued their work in the field of radioactivity. They have also carried out further research to improve understanding of the characteristics of nuclear reactions and radioactive elements.

Johann Bürgi, a pioneer in mathematics, tried to revolutionize the way triangulation functions are understood and applied. In his own words, Bürgi expressed his belief that the traditional methods used by his ancestors were cumbersome and laborious, and he aimed to develop a more efficient and accurate approach. Bürgi's innovative ideas were centered around the concept of dividing a right angle into multiple parts, allowing for the calculation of sines without the need for complex inscriptions of polygons. This breakthrough has the potential to simplify the search for triangular values and make them more accessible to a wider audience. His work culminated in the creation of his groundbreaking desks, which were published in his book The Astronomy Basis, in approximately 1586-1587. These tables represented a significant advancement in the field of trigonometry and laid the foundation for future developments in mathematics. It is important to note that Bürgi's work was not developed in isolation. His ideas were influenced by the work of other eminent mathematicians and astronomers, such as Tolemy in Almas and the mysterious Princeton 322, which is an ancient Babylon clay plate containing triangles. We initiated our study with a Grey Literature Review (GLR) to establish an initial understanding of the strategies employed by practitioners to manage flaky tests. The review was the basis for our subsequent analysis of disaster reduction and informed the design of our interviews. Our GLR is exploratory, not exhaustive and is intended to outline existing mitigation measures. We have complied with the established guidelines for conducting systematic reviews, focusing on materials detailing practitioners ' experiences and strategies in addressing premature issues, such as technical reports, presentations and blogs. Our search strategy produced 276,000 results, and we reduced the number of articles to 100 by improving Google search queries. We meticulously selected 56 articles written by practitioners that provided practical insights into flakiness mitigation, excluding theoretical discussions and research articles. In our analysis, we applied a quality assessment checklist to ensure the relevance and reliability of the selected articles. We have identified three key exclusion criteria: objectivity, adequacy of methodology and the adequacy of the topic, which has helped us to improve our choices to 38. Through the consensus process, we have consolidated the classification of mitigation measures described by practitioners, as detailed in table {ref{able: strategy} and discussed in section {ref{sec: outcome}. These insights open avenues for research that could assist practitioners in managing flakiness more effectively. Our introduction outlines the key role of software testing in modern development and the challenges posed by one-sided testing, which may weaken the developers ' confidence in the testing package and influence the quality of the software. We emphasized the prevalence and cost of reflective testing of large software systems and cited the experience of Google in implementing more than 50 million tests per day, as well as the large budget used to manage reflective testing. Our study builds on previous empirical research by examining the industrial context of flakiness and conducting qualitative analyses based on 14 practitioner interviews. Through this approach, we have sought to identify typical measures taken by practitioners and to explore how solutions can strengthen these practices. Our research issues guide our investigation into the localization of infertility, the perception of its effects by practitioners and the strategies adopted to mitigate its effects.

Cheesemakers have a long history of using colorants to enhance the appearance of their products. In times past, farmers would sometimes produce milk of lesser quality, which would result in a whiter cheese. To make this cheese more appealing to consumers, they began adding colorants to mimic the richer hues of higher-quality summer cheeses. Initially, these colorants were derived from natural sources such as saffron, marigold, and carrot juice. However, in the 17th century, the Dutch introduced a new colorant known as annatto. The Dutch had established colonies in Guyana and traded food, including annatto, with the indigenous communities. Anato, which is equivalent to “paint”, is purchased from the coastal areas of Guyana and Suriname and sold in the Netherlands by a trader authorized by the West India company, and “Huishoudelyk Woordboek” (Huseward Dictionary), a United States scientist at the University of Vermont, records that the first known series of documents on cheese dated back to 1743. Other historical documents from the same period confirm that the use of annatto, also referred to as "orleaan" or "orleans," to color cheese was already in practice by the mid-18th century. England is another country with a history of using annatto to color its cheeses. As early as the 16th century, colorants were added to Gloucester cheese to allow inferior cheese to be passed off as the superior Double Gloucester variety. Annatto was later adopted for this purpose as well. In summary, the use of colorants in cheese production has been a common practice for centuries, with annatto emerging as a popular choice due to its vibrant orange-red hue. This has increased the visual attractiveness of their products by cheese manufacturers and, in some cases, has deceived consumers into believing that they are buying higher-quality cheese.

Conifers and grasses are known for producing lightweight pollen, which is primarily dispersed by the wind to neighboring plants. This method of pollination is known as anemophily. On the contrary, some blooming plants have evolved into heavier, sticky pollen, specially suited for the transport of insects or larger animals. These pollinators, such as hummingbirds and bats, are often attracted by flowers that provide honey and pollen as incentives. As these animals move from one flower to another, they inadvertently transport pollen, leading to pollination. This process is known as entomophily. Fungi, on the other hand, have a diverse range of reproductive strategies. Most species of fungi can reproduce sexually, and their life cycles involve both haploid and diploid phases. These fungi are typically isogamous, meaning they do not exhibit male and female specialization. Instead, one haploid fungus grows into contact with another, and they fuse their cells. In some instances, the fusion may be asymmetric, with one cell donating only a nucleus, which could be considered a male role. Fungi may also possess more complex mating systems with additional sexes that do not fit the traditional male, female, or hermaphroditic classifications. Some fungi, such as baker's yeast, have mating types that determine compatibility. Beasts with the same matery type do not fuse into soak cells; only animals with different mating types do so. Many higher fungi produce mushrooms as part of their sexual reproduction process. Within the mushroom, diploid cells are formed, which later divide into haploid spores. A sexual system refers to the distribution of male and female reproductive structures within a species. This can vary widely across different organisms, from separate male and female individuals (dioecious) to hermaphroditic individuals that possess both male and female reproductive organs (monoecious). Understanding the sexuality systems of various organisms is essential for studying their reproductive biology, ecology and evolution.

\section*{Keywords} Stochastic dynamical systems, Neuronal network modeling, Asymptotic analysis, WKB approximation, Eikonal equations, Attractor escape. \section*{AMS classification} 37A50, 60G40, 92B25, 41A60 \section{Introduction} In this study, we delve into the intricate dynamics of stochastic dynamical systems, particularly focusing on the role of small noise perturbations. These perturbations can significantly alter system trajectories, enabling escape from stable attractor basins and inducing phenomena such as stochastic resonance and bifurcation shifts \cite{dykman1994observable, dykman1994large, maier1993, lindner2004, schimanskyGeier1985, arnold1979, arnold1990, Wihstutz_book2003}. Our research is particularly relevant in the context of biological neuronal networks, where noise is crucial for collective rhythms and synchronization \cite{Tsodyks1997, BrunelHakim1999, Hansel2001, Holcman_Tsodyks2006, Barak2007, daoduc2015}. We introduce a reduced stochastic dynamical system based on synaptic depression-facilitation, a model that captures the essence of neuronal network bursting activity \cite{Tsodyks1997, daoduc2015}. Our approach involves analyzing the distribution of interburst intervals, which correspond to escapes from an attractor. We have found that the rates of escape and the distribution of exit points can be determined by the approximate values of WKB, a method that provides insight into small noise restrictions (cite{Matkowsky1977exit, Schuss: Book, Schuss 1980, Bobrovsky Schusss1982). Our research has helped to understand the dynamics of escape in a system that is regularly driven, and the rate of escape is influenced by the intensity of the field (cite {smelyanskiy1999time, dykman2005}). We highlight the distinction between exiting and escaping, a clarification that is crucial for our analysis. The script is structured to introduce our reduced random models first and then explore a universal two-dimensional dynamic system with attractions and saddle points. We demonstrate that the maximum of the probability density function of trajectories before escape is shifted, depending on the noise amplitude $\sigma$. Our analysis ultimately looks at the escape from the attraction basin, where the trajectory can be re-entered several times before it finally escapes, a phenomenon that has an impact on the large tailings of the outbreak intervals observed in the experimental data (cite{rouach_CxKO}). \section{Modeling the Interburst Durations in Neuronal Networks} \subsection{Noisy Depression-Facilitation Model} Neuronal networks exhibit complex activity patterns, which can be modeled using mean-field models to represent the dynamics as stochastic differential equations. Bursting dynamics, characterized by transient periods of neuronal discharge, can be understood through the lens of short-term synaptic plasticity properties such as depression and facilitation \cite{Tsodyks1997, Barak2007, daoduc2015}. These properties are crucial for understanding the interburst periods, during which the network is relatively inactive. We focus on a depression-facilitation short-term synaptic plasticity model that describes network neuronal bursting \cite{Tsodyks1997, daoduc2015frontiers, Holcman_Tsodyks2006}. This model is represented by three equations for the mean voltage $h$, the depression $y$, and the facilitation $x$. The model incorporates the return to equilibrium, the increase in vesicular release probability, and the depletion of vesicular pools, all of which are essential for understanding the network activity. \subsection{Reduction to a Two-Dimensional System and Phase-Space Analysis} The system under consideration has three critical points: one attractor and two saddle-points. By reducing the system to a 2D-plane, we simplify the analysis while retaining the essential dynamics. The deterministic system, when reduced, has two attractors and one saddle-point. Our analysis reveals that the attractor's dynamics are anisotropic, with the eigenvalues indicating the stability and nature of the critical points. The escape dynamics from the attractor basin are characterized by trajectories that can reenter the basin multiple times before eventually escaping to infinity. This behavior is distinct from systems where escape ends upon the first encounter with the separatrix. Our study provides a novel explanation for the observed large tail distribution of interburst intervals in experimental time series, suggesting that each excursion outside and inside the basin of attraction contributes to an increased total escape time.

In this section, we present the Panel-Frozen Method (GSF), which is the most innovative and punitive method for estimating the sequence and composition of a limited mixture model. Given a random sample from an unknown true mixing measure \( G_0 \) with at most \( K_0 \) components, we propose a method to address overfitting issues associated with the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) when an upper bound \( K \geq K_0 \) is known. The overfitted MLE may converge slowly and include superfluous components, leading to an inconsistent estimate of \( K_0 \). Our Global Security Foundation approach provides for two types of punishment to address these issues: the near-zero mix of probabilities, and the near-location estimated atomic combination. We first identify a log-like function of initial punishment, which includes a non-negative punishment to ensure that the probability is mixed by the maximum, starting from zero, leading to a consistent estimate of the atoms. However, this preliminary estimate did not consistently estimate the order of the type II overpacking (K) because the type II overpacking was not addressed. In order to address this problem, we have introduced a fusion induction penalty for the distance between selected atoms, focusing on the continuous distance after the sorting process and not after all the equivalent distances, in order to reduce sensitivity to the \(K) selection. The GSF method relies on the concept of clustering, which groupes the atoms into groups, making internal distance within the cluster less than between the clusters. The method aims to merge estimates within each cluster to approximate the true atoms of \( G_0 \). To achieve this, we define a cluster ordering, a permutation of atoms that respects the cluster partition and is invariant to relabeling. The GSF method then fuses the ordered atoms within each cluster to produce a consistent estimator of both the order and components of the true mixing measure. The innovative aspects of our research include the introduction of a double penalized log-likelihood function that effectively addresses overfitting in mixture models, the development of a cluster partitioning strategy that enhances the estimation of the true atoms, and the use of cluster ordering to merge closely located atoms. Our method provides a significant advancement in the field of mixture model estimation, offering a more accurate and robust approach to estimating the underlying structure of the data.

According to van Heijenoort, a property is considered definite in Skolem's sense if it can be expressed by a well-formed formula in the simple predicate calculus of first order, where the only predicate constants are epsilon (ε) and possibly equality (=). In modern set theory, axiomatizations are typically embedded within a logical calculus framework. The formulation of the axiom of separation, which is crucial for defining subsets, is largely influenced by the approaches of Hermann Weyl and Skolem. It is important to note that the term has shifted from “potential function” to “formula”, “pre-production calculations”, “pre-production” and “logical calculation.” This shift is further elaborated in the section dealing with the concept of “functionality” in contemporary theory of creation. The history of the "ordered pair" concept is somewhat unclear. Gottlob Frege made an intuitive order in 1879 in two of its defined explanatory functions (A, B). This section introduces the methodology for estimating the parameters of the HIV transmission model using Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC). The average of the target distribution was estimated using the Nadaraya-Watson regression estimate, and statistics were calculated on median, pattern and credibility intervals. Cuba ' s HIV/AIDS data set for the period 1986-2007 is used for analysis and provides summary statistics based on testing time and methods. A comparison of the ABC and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMCC) methodology of the standard SIR model shows that ABC has the ability to replicate probabilities-based results under favourable conditions. The impact of tolerance rate on the posterior distribution is discussed, highlighting the tendency of ABC to produce larger tails compared to MCMC. The paper also addresses the challenge of the "curse of dimensionality" in ABC, where the bias may increase with the number of summary statistics. In order to alleviate this problem, it is proposed to undertake regression-based adjustments, including local linear and non-linear conditional super-peak returns, with the aim of matching distributions and compressing parameter estimates from the target distribution to approximate samples. The innovative aspects of this research include the application of ABC to the HIV transmission model, the comparison with MCMC methods, and the introduction of regression adjustments to address the curse of dimensionality. The results of the survey help to understand the parameter estimations of complex models in which direct probability-based extrapolations are challenging.

This section explores the competitive dynamics of the Wikipedia collaborative content creation process, where contributors often compete for content they produce. We draw on psychological ownership theory and territoriality theory to explain why contributors may develop a sense of ownership over Wikipedia articles or sections thereof, leading to competition and potential conflicts over the direction and content of these articles. The Wikipedia governance model, based on norms and policies developed by communities, plays a crucial role in mitigating these competitive trends. The Neutral Point of View (NPOV) principle is central to this model, promoting objectivity and preventing any single viewpoint from dominating an article. However, achieving NPOV can be challenging due to the complexity of issues, difficulty in verifying information, and intentional attempts by contributors to influence readers' perspectives. Our research aims to explore the interaction between competition dynamics and social technology governance mechanisms in the Wikipedia peer production process. We focus on two research issues: first, how do donors balance the costs and benefits of peer production and how do their editorial efforts relate to the fragmented ownership of articles? Second, how do governance mechanisms, particularly the enforcement of NPOV, affect the competitive dynamics and the relationship between contributors' editing efforts and content ownership? We propose a game-theoretic model to analyze competition and governance in Wikipedia's co-production process. This model will reflect the basic features of the system, taking into account both cooperative and competitive behaviour, and a better understanding of the complex interactions between donors and community governance mechanisms. The innovative aspect of our research is to review the dynamics of competition in the Wikipedia cooperation environment and to understand how these dynamics are influenced by community governance efforts, particularly with regard to the principles of the National Programme for the Prevention of Domestic Violence. By doing so, we aim to contribute to the literature on peer production and the socio-technical systems that underpin it.

This study introduces a novel Bayesian spatio-temporal approach to analyze respiratory prescription data at the General Practitioner (GP) surgery level in Scotland from 2015 to 2016. In Scotland, respiratory prescriptions account for 13 per cent of all prescription costs, highlighting the importance of understanding the factors affecting the distribution of prescriptions and the spatial differences in prescription rates. The unique characteristics of the data are point levels, but they are linked to fixed locations and are not feasible for forecasting in undetected locations, thus posing challenges. To address this, we proposed a finite dimensional process-convolution model that does not presuppose an underlying spatial process that is universally measurable. Our approach has advanced the current pattern of process evolution through a progressive random weighted plan that incorporates adaptive or local spatial structures. We provide open-source software to ensure the research is reproducible. The adaptive model significantly outperforms a simpler global smoothing model, leading to two principal findings. First, we establish a positive association between respiratory prescription rates and air pollution, particularly PM2.5. The increase of 1.23 ug/m3 in PM2.5 is related to a 2.2% increase in prescription charges. This finding is consistent with existing literature that associates air pollution with more severe health outcomes, such as hospitalization or death, and reinforces the evidence that air pollution significantly impacts respiratory health and associated healthcare costs, even at concentrations below legal limits. Second, the study revealed significant health inequities in the Scottish Health Board ' s respiratory prescription rate. Dumfries and Galloway and Greater Glasgow and Clyde have the highest mortality rates, with 27 per cent and 19 per cent, respectively, higher than the Scottish average. By contrast, Gramping and Okini have the lowest fertility rates, with a decline of 30 per cent and 40 per cent, respectively. These differences were evident both before and after the adjustment of known covariations, indicating that the health board residues had a significant impact on the respiratory prescription ratio. These results are vital for informing public health policy and resource allocation discussions, particularly in the context of ongoing debates sparked by the Marmot review in England and recent reports highlighting health inequalities. The study also opens avenues for future research, including the development of a multivariate extension of the model to explore inter-relationships between prescribing rates for different diseases and the creation of interactive software for data visualization to better communicate health inequalities to policymakers.

We propose an innovative approach to estimate the quantity \(\psi(P)\), which is dependent on the tail of a probability distribution \(P\). Instead of fitting \(P\) to a parametric distribution, we introduce an optimization problem that imposes a geometric shape condition on the tail of \(P\), defined by \(x \geq a\) for a sufficiently large threshold \(a\). This method ensures consistent extrapolation from the non-tail region and incorporates auxiliary constraints to provide additional information about \(P\). The question of optimization is intended to provide the upper level of trust for \\(\psi\) and is supported by statistical assurance that if the constraints on true distribution are maintained at \\(1\alpha\) confidence level (Ptext{ret}), the best value is the upper limit of real value, with at least the same level of trust. Our approach focuses on \(\psi(P)\) that represents either an expectation or a quantile of a random variable \(X\). We impose geometric conditions such as monotonicity and convexity on the tail of \(P\), which are common to most parametric distributions. In this paper, we look at the complex dynamics of the average curve flow, which is a fundamental process of geometric evolution, especially in the context of symmetric space. First of all, we introduced the concept of a medium curvature stream, which is a first-degree soaked layer, where the curvature vector evolves into multiple bodies. Our focus is on the evolution of submanifolds, specifically equifocal and proper complex equifocal submanifolds, which are generalizations of isoparametric submanifolds in Euclidean spaces to the more complex structure of symmetric spaces. Our survey is based on the previous work of Liu Teng and Terng-Thorbergsson, who explored the meso-curve prevalence of parity and plasma-levels in the initial data on Euclid and compact symmetric space, respectively. These studies revealed intriguing properties, such as the collapse of submanifolds to focal submanifolds and the existence of singularities under certain conditions. To broaden the scope of these concepts, we propose the concept of an appropriately complex balanced subsystem in asymmetrical types of symmetric space, characterized by its complex focus structure and a symmetrical grouping of actions. We highlight the importance of curvature-adapted submanifolds, which are those that align with the curvature of the ambient space, and their role as principal orbits in Hermann type actions. Our main contribution lies in the formulation and proof of a theorem that addresses the behavior of mean curvature flows with curvature-adapted proper complex equifocal submanifolds or their focal submanifolds as initial data in non-compact symmetric spaces, excluding hyperbolic spaces. This theory broadens the understanding of geometric evolution of the submagnetic layer under average curves and provides a deeper understanding of the interaction between submagnetic geometry and curves in environmental space. In summary, our paper presents a comprehensive exploration of the mean curvature flow of complex equifocal submanifolds in symmetric spaces, offering new perspectives on their geometric evolution and the underlying principles governing their behavior. Through rigorous mathematical analysis, we contribute to the field by elucidating the complex dynamics at play and setting the stage for further research in this area.

A prescription is a written order from a licensed healthcare professional, such as a physician or dentist, authorizing a patient to receive a specific pharmaceutical product. It typically includes various legal requirements, such as a registration number, for example, a DEA (Drug Enforcement Administration) Number in the United States. Each prescription is unique to the patient and contains the patient's name. In the United Kingdom and Ireland, the patient's name and address are also required. The prescription is dated, and some jurisdictions may impose a time limit on its validity. Historically, prescriptions include the pharmacist ' s instructions for synthetic drugs. However, most modern prescriptions specify pre-manufactured pharmaceutical products that require minimal or no preparation by the pharmacist. The directions for the patient to follow when taking the medication are printed on the label of the pharmaceutical product. The term "prescription" originates from the Latin words "pre-" (meaning "before") and "script" (meaning "writing" or "written"). This reflects the fact that a prescription is an order that must be documented before a drug can be dispensed. In the industry, prescriptions are often colloquially referred to as "scripts." A prescription typically contains the following information: - The healthcare professional who prescribed the medication - The patient for whom the prescription is valid - The specific pharmaceutical product prescribed In some cases, additional information may be required depending on the jurisdiction, type of drug, or patient group. For instance, many brand-name drugs have cheaper generic alternatives that are therapeutically and biochemically equivalent. Prescription may also include an explanation as to whether the prescription allows generic equivalent alternatives. In summary, a prescription is a crucial document that ensures patients receive the appropriate medication as directed by a healthcare professional. It contains essential information and may include specific instructions regarding drug equivalence and substitution.

Induction motors are known for their significant reactive component, which results in a low power factor. This low power factor resulted in an increase in passive currents extracted from the electricity supply, resulting in further loss of the power system. To alleviate this problem, industrial plants can use synchronized engines to provide the necessary reaction power for induction engines. This approach enhanced the overall power coefficient of the plant and reduced the passive currents extracted from the grid. Synchronization condenser is a synchronized engine designed for power coefficient correction. They offer seamless, automatic power factor correction and can generate up to 150% additional reactive power (vars). These devices are not subject to the electrical waves of the system and can sometimes be absorbed. Synchronous condensers do not produce switching transients, excessive voltage levels, or electrical resonances. The rotational inertia of synchronized condensers enables them to provide limited voltage support when the short current falls. Introduced in the 1930s and widely used in the 1950s, synchronous condensers were eventually replaced by static var compensators (SVCs) in new installations due to their higher costs. However, they remain a viable alternative or supplement to capacitors for power factor correction, especially in situations where harmonics have caused capacitor overheating and failures. Synchronization condensers also support voltage levels. The reactive power provided by a capacitor bank is directly proportional to the square of its terminal voltage. This relationship highlights the importance of maintaining appropriate voltage levels for optimal performance and efficiency in power systems.

In this study, we have systematically investigated the impact of five key factors on the resolution of LFOCDHM digital ultrascope (LFOCDHM) imaging. These factors include the sample-to-sensor distance, the spatial and temporal coherence of the illumination, the finite size of the sensor pixels, and the finite extent of the image sub-field of view (sub-FOV) used for reconstruction. Our analysis and experiments revealed that the sensor pixel size is the most significant factor limiting the imaging resolution of LFOCDHM systems. The side effects from other experimental factors are relatively manageable. For instance, using a laser as an ideal temporally coherent light source and increasing the source-to-sample distance can approximate an ideal spatially coherent source. Employing pixel super-resolution (SR) algorithms can reduce the effective size of the imaging sensor. However, even with these measures, using an imaging sensor with smaller pixel size can still enhance the quality of the SR reconstructions. Specifically, if the desired resolution is around $1 \mu m$, the up-sampling factor $w$ will vary for different pixel sizes. When pixel size is close to the desired resolution, the sampling coefficient (w$) will be smaller and less information will be needed for reconstruction. Conversely, a higher upscaling factor (for larger pixel sizes), even using a pixel SR re-engineering algorithm, would result in more faults that could not be bridged across frequency gaps. Therefore, for LFOCDHM techniques, a smaller pixel size is crucial for achieving higher resolution and requires less information to reach the expected super-resolved resolution. Additionally, using LED as the light source can make the system more compact, portable, and cost-effective. However, the coherence length of the LED will also affect the reconstructed resolution. According to our equations, increasing ${z_1}$ and decreasing ${z_2}$ can effectively improve the coherence of light sources and enhance the imaging resolution. Furthermore, decreasing ${z_2}$ can reduce the reconstructed area when the desired resolution is determined. Our analysis of these parameters based on transfer functions has provided a quantitative resolution limit determined by the minimum first cut-off frequency of these transfer functions. This quantitative relationship allows for preliminary estimates of the ultimate resolution after employing SR methods. Thus, the derived theoretical models can offer valuable guidance in selecting appropriate system parameters to achieve higher imaging resolution. In order to validate the theoretical model, we have used variable control methods, changing only one or two parameters in each experiment. Resolution targets are used to quantify imaging resolution, and the results of the experiment confirm the validity of our theoretical model. It is important to note that while this work demonstrates how our theoretical models can be utilized to improve imaging resolution by optimizing the optical design of a LFOCDHM system, it may also be possible to counteract the effects of these imperfect system parameters through computational approaches. Based on the transfer functions we have derived, we can establish the forward image formation model (from object to image) for a given LFOCDHM system. Then, certain mathematical algorithms can be adopted to recover the ideal object information from the actual measurement, i.e., to solve the corresponding inverse problem. In our future work, we will focus on the reduction of resolutions related to those factors and on addressing their adverse effects through the reprocessing algorithms.
